eras.era: Urartu (Biainili, forerunner kingdom of the Armenian highlands) vs the Neo-Assyrian Empire, 8th century BC. Level depicts Tiglath-pileser III's campaign to Tushpa, 735 BC
eras.dateRange: 743 BC: Tiglath-pileser III defeats Sarduri II and his allies in the land of Kummuh (Commagene), between Kishtan and Halpi. 735 BC (Eponym Chronicle, year of Assur-shallimanni, entry 'to Urartu'): the Assyrian campaign reaches Tushpa (Assyrian Turushpa). By Tiglath-pileser's own annals, Sarduri is confined in the city, the Assyrians fight before its gates and set up a royal image facing it; the citadel is not taken. 735 is the standard date; other dates for the Turushpa raid that circulate in secondary sources (736, or soon after 743) are unverified. 714 BC: Sargon II's eighth campaign. Rusa is defeated at Mount Uaush (Wa'ush), and Musasir (Urartian Ardini) and Haldi's temple are sacked later in the same campaign; Sargon's later inscriptions claim that Rusa then killed himself. The level depicts 735 BC.

briefing.title: The Rock of Tushpa
briefing.body:
Biainili, the kingdom Assyria calls Urartu, is the forerunner kingdom of the Armenian highlands. Its kings have raised fortresses from Lake Van to the plain of the Araxes, where Argishti I founded Erebuni. Their capital, Tushpa, crowns a sheer rock on the eastern shore of Lake Van. In their annals, the god Haldi goes forth with his weapon.

In 743 BC Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria broke King Sarduri II and his allies in Kummuh, and by the Assyrian account Sarduri escaped by night on a mare. Now, around 735 BC, the Assyrian king has marched into the heart of Biainili with his standing army. He brings spearmen in pointed helmets, archers behind tall siege shields, horsemen riding in pairs, and wheeled battering rams like those carved on his palace walls at Nimrud.

Sarduri is shut inside Tushpa. The Assyrians will fight before its gates and raise an image of their king facing the city. But no Assyrian army has stood beneath this rock before, and its citadel rises high above the lake.

Commander, the beacons are lit. Put bowmen in bronze helmets on the walls, rain stones and firebrands on the rams, and keep the gate of Tushpa shut. Let Tiglath-pileser raise his image before the walls. He will not take the rock. Hold Tushpa, as Sarduri's garrison held it.
briefing.stakes: Hold the citadel of Tushpa, royal seat of Biainili, until Tiglath-pileser III's army gives up and withdraws.
briefing.victoryEpilogue: The rock held, as it did in history. By his own annals Tiglath-pileser III beat the Urartians before the gates and set up his royal image facing Tushpa, but he did not take the citadel, and no Assyrian army reached the Urartian capital again. Biainili endured into the 7th century BC, outlasting even Sargon II's victory over King Rusa at Mount Uaush and his sack of Haldi's temple at Musasir in 714 BC.
briefing.defeatEpilogue: Tushpa falls here, but it did not fall in history. In 735 BC the Assyrians claimed victory before the gates, yet the citadel on its rock held and Tiglath-pileser III withdrew without taking it. Rally the garrison and hold where Sarduri's defenders held.
didYouKnow: The Urartian kings called their realm Biainili. 'Urartu' is the name the Assyrians used.
Yerevan traces its founding to Erebuni, the fortress Argishti I, father of Sarduri II, built in 782 BC.
Bronze helmets and quivers found at Karmir Blur, near Yerevan, bear inscriptions naming Urartian kings, among them Sarduri son of Argishti.
Urartian forts passed warnings from hill to hill by fire beacon. A 2015 GIS study of Early Iron Age and Urartian sites in Armenia argued that the beacon network was deliberately planned.
There were no catapults yet: Greek sources date the first mechanical artillery to Syracuse in 399 BC, more than three centuries after this campaign.
Sarduri II's annals were inscribed on a stele set in one of the great rock-cut niches at Hazine Kapisi, on the north face of the Rock of Van.

keyFigures.name: Sarduri II (Urartian: Sarduri Argishtihi, 'Sarduri son of Argishti')
keyFigures.role: King of Biainili (Urartu), defender of Tushpa
keyFigures.note: Son of Argishti I. Reign dates vary: c. 755 to 735 BC (Britannica), c. 756 to c. 730 BC and c. 763 to 735 BC (other estimates). Defeated in 743 BC in Kummuh; Tiglath-pileser III's annals say he was confined in Turushpa in 735 BC, and the citadel was not taken. His annals were inscribed on a stele set in the western niche at Hazine Kapisi on the Rock of Van. A helmet and a quiver inscribed with his name are reported from Teishebaini (Karmir Blur). Recommended in-game hero for this era.

keyFigures.name: Tiglath-pileser III
keyFigures.role: King of Assyria (r. 745 to 727 BC)
keyFigures.note: Traditionally credited with building Assyria's standing army of professional soldiers (Radner). Beat Sarduri II's coalition in 743 BC. His annals say that in 735 BC he shut Sarduri up in Turushpa, inflicted a heavy defeat before the city gates and set up his royal image facing the city. He did not capture the citadel. Radner reports that an official afterwards urged him to attack Turushpa again to immortalise his name; he did not. Recommended level boss.

keyFigures.name: Mati'-ilu (Mati'-el) of Arpad (Bit-Agusi)
keyFigures.role: North Syrian king allied with Sarduri II
keyFigures.note: Member of the anti-Assyrian coalition led by Sarduri II that Tiglath-pileser III defeated in Kummuh in 743 BC. Background figure only.

keyFigures.name: Argishti I
keyFigures.role: King of Biainili, father of Sarduri II
keyFigures.note: Founded Erebuni (782 BC) and Argishtihinili (commonly dated 776 BC) in the Araxes valley. Background figure only; reign dates vary by source.

keyFigures.name: Rusa (son of Sarduri, conventionally Rusa I)
keyFigures.role: King of Biainili after Sarduri II
keyFigures.note: The traditional view (Britannica, eCUT) makes him Sargon II's opponent in 714 BC, defeated at Mount Uaush. Sargon's later inscriptions claim Rusa killed himself with his own iron dagger. Michael Roaf (in Biainili-Urartu, Acta Iranica 51, 2012) argues that the 714 opponent may have been Rusa son of Erimena and questions the suicide claim. Relevant only if a 714 BC level is made.

keyFigures.name: Sargon II
keyFigures.role: King of Assyria (r. 722 to 705 BC)
keyFigures.note: His eighth campaign (714 BC) is recorded in the Letter to the god Ashur (Louvre AO 5372): victory at Mount Uaush and the sack of Musasir. He is not part of the 735 BC level.

keyFigures.name: Urzana
keyFigures.role: Ruler of Musasir (Urartian Ardini), keeper of Haldi's temple
keyFigures.note: Sargon sacked his city in 714 BC and carried off his family and the statue and treasure of Haldi. Background figure only.

keyFigures.name: Haldi
keyFigures.role: Chief god of Biainili
keyFigures.note: Shown as a man, with or without wings, standing on a lion. Urartian annals repeat the formula that Haldi 'went forth with his weapon'. His great temple stood at Musasir. Use him as the theme of the support tower, not as a unit.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: Radner (Assyrian Empire Builders, 'The Assyrian army') describes Tiglath-pileser III's standing army of professional and mercenary soldiers, with infantry split into archers and spearmen. Neo-Assyrian reliefs show spearmen in pointed helmets carrying large round shields.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Pointed conical metal helmet. Lamellar or scale corselet to the waist over a knee-length tunic. Large round, slightly convex shield. Thrusting spear about head height plus a short sword. Curled beard. Use iron-grey and bronze metal tones on undyed tunics. Exact uniform colours are unverified, so avoid strong team colours.
enemyRoster.justification: Standard Assyrian line infantry of the 8th century BC, attested for Tiglath-pileser III's army. The annals do not list unit types for the 735 campaign, so their presence at Tushpa is inferred from the army's normal composition.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: A British Museum relief of Tiglath-pileser III (catalogued as W_1849-0502-10 in the research pass; number not re-verified) shows a pair of armoured cavalrymen riding down an enemy horseman, one spearing the enemy horse. Radner notes that Assyrian cavalry first fought in pairs (one rider shooting, the other holding the reins of both horses).
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Ride in pairs: one rider with a long lance, the partner with a composite bow. Pointed helmet with earflaps, fringed tunic decorated with discs set in squares, cuirass. Horses have the triple tassel on top of the head and tassels on a plaited collar. Riders sit on a saddle-cloth with no stirrups.
enemyRoster.justification: Cavalry was a growing arm of Tiglath-pileser III's army, and his own reliefs show the pair formation with a lancer. Fast, light unit; presence at Tushpa inferred, not recorded.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: A British Museum relief of Tiglath-pileser III (registration number unconfirmed) shows archers attacking a city from behind a tall siege shield whose squared top folds back. The museum describes this shape as characteristic of his reign.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Man-height wicker or reed siege shield with a squared top return angled backward, carried by a shield-bearer. Behind it, one or two archers in long garments with broad fringed girdles and round caps or helmets with earflaps; one bearded archer also carries a sword. The unit moves as one block, with the shield always facing the towers.
enemyRoster.justification: The unit type is attested for this reign, but no source records siege-shield archers at Tushpa; the annals describe a battle before the gates. The shield works naturally as frontal armour against arrows.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: Reliefs from Tiglath-pileser III's palace at Nimrud show a four-wheeled ram battering city walls from a ramp. The water-ladle crew detail comes from Sennacherib's Lachish relief (701 BC), a later reign of the same Neo-Assyrian army, which shows a soldier ladling water over a ram's front against torches thrown by defenders.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Boxy wooden hull covered in hides or wicker on four wheels, with a short domed turret at the front and a ram beam with a metal head. Escorted by crewmen carrying long-handled ladles and water. Do not use the six-wheeled ram-tower: it belongs to Ashurnasirpal II's 9th-century reliefs, over a century earlier.
enemyRoster.justification: Four-wheeled rams are attested in Tiglath-pileser III's own reliefs, but no source says rams were used at Tushpa, and the annals record a battle before the gates rather than an assault on the citadel. Treat their presence as a reasonable reconstruction. This unit carries the era mechanic described in mechanicAudit.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: A British Museum relief of Ashurnasirpal II (North-West Palace, Nimrud, 9th c. BC) shows Assyrian soldiers crossing a river on inflated animal skins, blowing into them to stay afloat. Separately, Sargon II's Letter to Ashur (714 BC) boasts that he made his chariots, cavalry and troops 'fly over' Mount Simirria 'like eagles'.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Soldiers half-submerged, chests on inflated goat-skins, some blowing into the skin's leg. Bows and quivers held clear of the water. They cross Lake Van on a water lane instead of the road. Use V-shaped wakes and ripples to show the 'airborne' state.
enemyRoster.justification: Deliberate game license. No Assyrian unit flew, and nothing records skin-floats at Tushpa or on Lake Van; the attested image is 9th century. It is the least bad option because the method is attested in Assyrian art, it suits a lakeside map, and it explains why only direct-fire towers (bows, javelins) can hit these units while lobbed stones and the fire tower cannot. Alternative name: 'Ashur's Eagles' (cliff-scalers), from Sargon's own metaphor, but that phrase belongs to 714 BC, not 735 BC.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: His annals (RINAP 1, Tadmor and Yamada 2011; older translation in Luckenbill, ARAB I) say he shut Sarduri up in Turushpa, inflicted a heavy defeat before the city gates, and set up his royal image facing the city. Nimrud reliefs show him in his chariot under a tasselled state parasol held by a eunuch attendant.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Small, low royal chariot; copy the number of horses from the specific relief used as reference (team size in this reign is unverified). Charioteer at the king's side, eunuch attendant holding a tasselled parasol over him. The king wears the royal hat and a long fringed robe. Shield-bearer guards walk alongside. Suggested ability 'Royal Image': at 50% HP he halts for 4 s and erects a stele (300 HP). While the stele stands, all Assyrian units get +15% move speed. Destroying the stele removes the buff.
enemyRoster.justification: He is the commander named in the Assyrian account of the Tushpa campaign. The annals use the first-person royal voice, so his personal presence is what the source claims rather than an independently confirmed fact. The stele ability comes straight from the annals.

towerAudit.reason: Archery is well attested in Biainili. A bronze quiver inscribed with Sarduri II's name is reported from Teishebaini (Karmir Blur); its present museum is not confirmed in this pass. Inscribed arrowheads, quivers and other weapons were dedicated in Urartian temples.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: Square tower with a stone base and crenellated top. Archers wear conical bronze helmets, carry composite bows and bronze quivers with relief friezes, and have round bronze shields with lion and bull bands leaning against the parapet.

towerAudit.reason: Mechanical artillery did not exist in 735 BC. Diodorus places the first catapult, a non-torsion bow-machine (gastraphetes or katapeltikon), at Syracuse under Dionysius I in 399 BC, and Marsden follows him. Torsion engines are traditionally dated to c. 340 BC under Philip II of Macedon. A bolt-thrower at Tushpa would be more than 330 years too early.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: Projecting stone bastion where Urartian spearmen in conical bronze helmets hurl heavy spears down at single targets, with racks of spears beside them. Urartian riders on bronze belts carry one or two spears, and spears were dedicated to Haldi. Throwing spears from walls is plausible but not specifically attested, so this is acceptable license.

towerAudit.reason: Same dating as the ballista: no mechanical stone-thrower before 399 BC, and no torsion machine before c. 340 BC. Assyrian siege reliefs (from Ashurnasirpal II's 9th-century series onward) show defenders throwing stones down from their turrets onto attackers, which fills the same splash-damage role.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: Crenellated parapet stacked with boulders. Two or three defenders heave stones over the edge, which land in an area of effect on the path below. Use weathered pale-grey rock for the Rock of Van (exact rock type unverified).

towerAudit.reason: A 'fire altar' suggests the Iranian fire cult of much later periods. The Urartian Haldi cult is known from tower temples (susi), animal sacrifice and weapon dedications; the sources consulted show no Urartian fire-altar cult (unverified absence, not proof). Fire as a weapon is still historical: Urartian fortresses ran a fire-beacon signal network (Earley-Spadoni 2015; beacon fires also appear in the account of Sargon's 714 campaign), and the Lachish relief (701 BC) shows defenders throwing burning torches at Assyrian rams.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: Hilltop signal tower with a raised fuel platform and a big bonfire. Defenders light brands from the beacon and hurl them, setting a burn effect. Smoke columns can link visually to other beacons on the far ridges.

towerAudit.reason: The sources consulted do not confirm drums in Urartian warfare (unverified). That makes the drum an unsupported choice rather than a proven anachronism. A better-grounded aura for Biainili is the Haldi cult: Urartian annals repeat that 'Haldi went forth with his weapon', and temples were filled with dedicated shields, spears, helmets and quivers.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: Small square tower-shrine (susi) with dedicated bronze shields bearing concentric lion and bull bands, and a tall spear standard in front. Give the aura ring a warm bronze glow. Haldi can appear as a figure standing on a lion on a shield boss, never as a combat unit.

mechanicAudit.existingMechanic: Assyrian era: battering rams that repair or are repaired.
mechanicAudit.reason: Wheeled rams are attested for this army (a four-wheeled ram on a ramp in Tiglath-pileser III's Nimrud reliefs). Free self-repair has no basis in the sources. What the reliefs do show is a crew protecting the engine: at Lachish (701 BC, Sennacherib, a later reign of the same Neo-Assyrian army) a soldier ladles water over the ram's front against defenders' torches. Tying repair to a visible, killable crew keeps the mechanic, rests it on evidence, and gives the player a counter. The Rock of Van itself proved impregnable (Radner), so rams should threaten only the gate.
mechanicAudit.proposal: Wheeled Battering Ram: HP 1400; speed 0.5x Assyrian Spearmen; takes 50% damage from Biainili Bowmen and Javelin Bastion (hide-and-wicker housing), 100% from Stone-Hurlers' Parapet, 125% from Beacon Tower burn. Ram crew: each ram spawns with 2 Water-Bearers (HP 80 each, same speed, walk directly behind). While at least one Water-Bearer lives: (a) any burn on the ram ends after 1.5 s instead of its normal duration; (b) if the ram takes no damage for 3 s, it regains 2% of max HP per second, up to 60% of max HP. Killing both Water-Bearers turns off both effects for that ram. Gate assault: a ram that reaches the gate does not leak at once. It stops and batters, costing 1 life every 4 s (maximum 5 lives) until destroyed. Tushpa rule: rams can only use the gate lane; the cliff faces of the citadel cannot be battered.

eras.heroNote: Vardan Mamikonian (Mamikonean) is not appropriate here. He was killed at the battle of Avarayr in 451 AD (Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Avarayr'), about 1,185 years after this campaign; the exact day is given differently in sources, so only the year is used. The period-correct hero is Sarduri II (Urartian 'Sarduri Argishtihi', Sarduri son of Argishti), King of Biainili, reigning c. 755 to 735 BC per Britannica, with other estimates of c. 756 to c. 730 BC and c. 763 to 735 BC. He is the king Tiglath-pileser III's annals say was shut inside Turushpa in 735 BC. Visual sources: bronze helmets and a bronze quiver from Karmir Blur (Teishebaini) inscribed with his name. Suggested in-game title: 'Sarduri, son of Argishti, King of Biainili'. The fuller title 'king of the land of Biainili, lord of the city of Tushpa' is documented here on a shield of his son Rusa; Sarduri II's own titulary was not checked in this pass, so use it for Sarduri only as stylization. For a 714 BC level the hero would be Rusa (son of Sarduri), noting Roaf's 2012 argument that Sargon's opponent may have been Rusa son of Erimena.

mapRecommendation.reason: Tushpa (Van), the Urartian capital, stands on a long, isolated rock ridge, more than a kilometre long and roughly 80 to 100 m high (published figures vary), by the eastern shore of Lake Van. The 735 BC campaign, the first and only time an Assyrian army reached Tushpa (Radner), happened exactly here. The lakeside setting also supports the Skin-Float Raiders water lane.
mapRecommendation.mapAnachronisms: Tushpa Vale: correct for the era. Use 'Tushpa' (Urartian) or 'Turushpa' (Assyrian). Assyrian texts speak of a 'Sea of Nairi', usually identified with Lake Van (some scholars prefer Lake Urmia for some passages); 'Thospitis' is a later Greek name derived from Tushpa. Remove the later medieval and Ottoman structures of Van Fortress; show Urartian walls of large stone blocks like Sarduri I's wall at the western foot of the citadel, whose inscription says he brought the stone blocks from the city of Alniunu. Gyumri Road: 'Gyumri' is a much later name (renamed Alexandropol in 1837 and Leninakan 1924 to 1990). One scholarly view derives the region's name, Shirak, from 'Eriahi', a land whose conquest Argishti I records; a period label would be 'Eriahi Road'. The claims that 'Kumayri' appears in 8th-c. BC Urartian inscriptions and that Cimmerians founded it c. 720 BC are unverified and must not be used. Araxes Crossing: the valley fits the era: Argishti I founded Erebuni (782 BC) and Argishtihinili (commonly dated 776 BC), which was fed by canals from the Araxes. 'Araxes' is a Greek form, and the Urartian name of the river is unverified; 'Argishtihinili Fields' is a safe period label. Lori Gates: the monasteries are anachronistic by about 1,700 years (Sanahin founded in the 10th c. AD; Haghpat built 10th to 13th c. AD). Swap them for Iron Age hill-forts and beacon platforms. Whether Lori lay inside Urartian control in 735 BC is unverified (low confidence: at or beyond the northern frontier).

claims.claim: Urartu's center lay in the Armenian highland between Lakes Van, Urmia and Sevan; Urartian sources from the 9th century BC call it Biainili, and Assyrian sources first call the region the 'Nairi countries'.

Not re-verifiable here, so the palu number and the 'counted from 744' line are removed, and the date now rests on the Eponym Chronicle entry for 735 (Assur-shallimanni, 'to Urartu').

The day and year come from one unrefetched excerpt, and the suicide is Sargon's claim, which Roaf disputes. Changed to 'later in the same campaign' and 'Sargon's later inscriptions claim that Rusa then killed himself'; claim confidence set to low.

eras.era: Sasanian Persia vs the Armenian nakharars of Persarmenia: the Vardanank revolt (edict 449, armed revolt 450-451) and its sequel, Vahan Mamikonian's war (481/482-484)
eras.dateRange: Yazdegerd II's edict imposing Zoroastrianism and the Artashat assembly: 449. Armed revolt: 450-451. Battle of Avarayr: 451, dated 26 May (Armenian church tradition and older scholarship such as Kurkjian; also Wikipedia 'Churs') or 2 June (current Wikipedia 'Battle of Avarayr', 'Vardan Mamikonian', 'Yazdegerd II', 'Mihr-Narseh'); no source I could read settles it. 2 June 451 was not Pentecost: by the Alexandrian Easter reckoning Easter 451 fell on 8 April, so Pentecost was 27 May. Leontine martyrs executed 455 (454 in some sources). Vahan Mamikonian's revolt: 481/482-484. Treaty of Nvarsak: 484. Vahan appointed marzpan: 485.

briefing.title: Vardanants: The Stand at Avarayr
briefing.dateline: Plain of Avarayr, Artaz, spring 451 AD
briefing.body:
Plain of Avarayr, spring of 451. Two years ago the King of Kings, Yazdegerd II, commanded the Armenians to forsake Christ for the Zoroastrian faith of his court. From Artashat, Armenia's bishops and princes answered: loyalty to the King, and loyalty to their faith. Summoned to his court, the princes were forced to bow; back home, they renounced that conversion and took up arms.

Now the King's general, Mushkan Niusalavurt, comes with the armored horsemen of the Immortals and a corps of war elephants. Vardan Mamikonian, sparapet of Armenia, has drawn up the princes' contingents on the banks of the Tghmut river in the land of Artaz. No help is coming: Emperor Marcian has refused the Armenian appeal. And Vasak of Siwnik, the marzpan, has gone over to the Persians with several noble houses.

On the eve of battle the priest Ghevond spoke to the army, and the soldiers received communion.

History records what followed. The Armenians held their ground until the Persians brought their elephants forward. Vardan fell with eight of his commanders, and Yeghishe counts 1,036 Armenian dead. The field was Persia's, but it cost Persia dearly, and the defiance did not die with Vardan. Thirty-three years later his nephew Vahan Mamikonian won the Treaty of Nvarsak, and with it freedom of worship for Armenia.

Yeghishe wrote that death understood is immortality. This is your hour, defender of the highlands. Stand with Vardan where history wavered. Hold the river, break the elephants, and keep the line.
briefing.stakes: Hold the plain of Avarayr against Yazdegerd II's army and defend Armenia's right to keep its Christian faith.
briefing.victoryEpilogue: You held the Tghmut line. History was harder: at the real Avarayr the Persians won the field, and Vardan fell with eight of his commanders and, by Yeghishe's count, 1,036 Armenians. But the victory cost Persia dearly, and the struggle went on until 484, when Vahan Mamikonian's renewed revolt ended in the Treaty of Nvarsak and freedom of worship for Armenia.
briefing.defeatEpilogue: The line breaks, as it broke in 451 when the Persian elephants were brought forward and Vardan fell. Yet Avarayr did not end the struggle: Vardan's nephew Vahan Mamikonian rose again, and in 484 the Treaty of Nvarsak gave Armenia freedom of worship.
didYouKnow: The Armenian Church honors Vardan and his companions as saints on Vardanants, kept on the last Thursday before Great Lent.
The Tghmut river of Avarayr is today's Zangmar, which flows past Maku in northwestern Iran into the Araxes.
Ammianus Marcellinus, a Roman officer who marched against Persia in 363, wrote that Persian horsemen were so fully plated that arrows could lodge only at the eye-holes and nostrils.
In 450 a Zoroastrian fire temple was installed inside Etchmiadzin Cathedral; excavators in the 1950s found its remains beneath the altar of the east apse.
Ammianus says the stone-thrower of his day was called the onager, the wild ass, because wild asses kick stones back at the hunters chasing them.
Ammianus reports that Persian elephant drivers carried a knife bound to the right hand, to kill a maddened elephant before it could trample its own side.

keyFigures.name: Vardan Mamikonian (Vardan Mamikonean)
keyFigures.role: Sparapet (hereditary supreme commander), head of the Mamikonian house, leader of the 450-451 revolt
keyFigures.note: Born c. 387 at Ashtishat in Taron (approximate); killed at Avarayr in 451. Son of Hamazasp Mamikonian and Sahakanoysh, daughter of Catholicos Sahak, so Sahak's grandson. Venerated as a saint of the Armenian Apostolic Church (Vardanants).

keyFigures.name: Hmayeak Mamikonian
keyFigures.role: Vardan's brother; father of Vahan
keyFigures.note: Led the Armenian embassy to Emperor Theodosius II in 450; killed in Tayk in the fighting after Avarayr.

keyFigures.name: Vasak Siwni
keyFigures.role: Lord of Siwnik; marzpan of Persian Armenia from 442
keyFigures.note: Sat in the 449 Artashat assembly, then led the pro-Persian faction; several noble houses went over with him before or during the battle (accounts differ). Yeghishe and Ghazar Parpetsi tell the aftermath differently, but in both he ends imprisoned. Died 452.

keyFigures.name: Mushkan Niusalavurt
keyFigures.role: Commander of the Sasanian army sent against the rebels, appointed by Mihr-Narseh
keyFigures.note: His army included the Immortals and war elephants. He survived Avarayr heavily wounded. Per Ghazar he was dismissed and sent home after reporting the Persian losses; per Yeghishe he gave Vasak free rein, and the turmoil that followed led to Vasak's imprisonment.

keyFigures.name: Yazdegerd II
keyFigures.role: Sasanian King of Kings (r. 438 or 439 to 457)
keyFigures.note: Issued the 449 edict imposing Zoroastrianism on Armenia. After Avarayr he appointed Adhur-Hormizd marzpan and ended the persecution in Armenia, but the clergy held captive in Persia were later executed.

keyFigures.name: Mihr-Narseh (Mehr-Narseh)
keyFigures.role: Wuzurg framadar (chief minister) of Yazdegerd II
keyFigures.note: Of the House of Suren; the edict to the Armenians went out in his name, and he appointed Mushkan to command.

keyFigures.name: Adhur-Hormizd (Atrormizd)
keyFigures.role: Marzpan of Armenia appointed in 451
keyFigures.note: Sent after Avarayr with instructions to allow freedom of worship; his appointment ended the persecution in Armenia for the time being.

keyFigures.name: Ghevond (Leontius) of Vanand
keyFigures.role: Priest; spiritual leader of the rebel army
keyFigures.note: Addressed the army on the eve of Avarayr. Taken captive to Persia and executed with Catholicos Hovsep and other clergy (the Leontine martyrs) in 455 (454 in some sources).

keyFigures.name: Catholicos Hovsep I
keyFigures.role: Catholicos of Armenia (437-452)
keyFigures.note: Acting head of the Church at the 449 Artashat assembly of nobles and clergy that answered the edict; among the Leontine martyrs.

keyFigures.name: Emperor Marcian
keyFigures.role: East Roman emperor (450-457)
keyFigures.note: The Armenian embassy of 450 first reached Theodosius II, who received it favorably but died. Marcian, advised by Anatolius and Florentius not to fight Persia, refused help.

keyFigures.name: Vahan Mamikonian
keyFigures.role: Son of Hmayeak, nephew of Vardan; leader of the 481/482-484 revolt; marzpan from 485
keyFigures.note: Born c. 440/445, died c. 503/510. Won at Akori and at Nersehapat in Artaz (482/483), lost at Akesga; after Peroz died in 484 his rising ended in the Treaty of Nvarsak. Asked Ghazar Parpetsi to write his History.

keyFigures.name: Balash (Valash)
keyFigures.role: Sasanian King of Kings (r. 484-488)
keyFigures.note: Brother and successor of Peroz I, who was killed by the Hephthalites in 484. The Treaty of Nvarsak was concluded between Vahan and Balash's representatives.

keyFigures.name: Yeghishe (Elishe, Ełišē)
keyFigures.role: Historian, author of the History of Vardan and the Armenian War
keyFigures.note: Main narrative source for Avarayr. Tradition makes him Vardan's secretary, but the date of composition is debated (5th century vs later). English translation by R. W. Thomson (1982).

keyFigures.name: Ghazar Parpetsi (Łazar P'arpec'i)
keyFigures.role: Historian, History of Armenia (c. 500)
keyFigures.note: Second main account of 449-451 and main source for Vahan's war and Nvarsak; written at Vahan Mamikonian's request after 493.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: The paygan were the conscript infantry who made up the bulk of Sasanian foot, armed with light wooden or wicker shields, leather caps and short spears. Ammianus Marcellinus (24.6.8, campaign of 363) describes Persian infantry advancing in very close order behind oblong, curved shields covered with wickerwork and raw hides, with elephants behind them.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Knee-length belted tunic and loose trousers in undyed wool and earth tones; boiled-leather cap (a few simple iron helmets); tall oblong curved shield of wicker faced with tan rawhide; short thrusting spear. Move in tight blocks. Avoid Achaemenid Persepolis-style 'Immortal' imagery, which is nearly a thousand years too early.
enemyRoster.justification: Sasanian infantry is well attested in the 4th-6th centuries, but no source I could read describes the infantry at Avarayr itself; its presence there is inferred.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: The aswaran, cavalry furnished by the aristocracy, were the backbone of the Sasanian army; they wore mail, ranged from archers to fully armored lancers, and were famed for archery. Lighter-equipped riders give the fast archetype.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Rider in mail shirt over a tunic, unarmored or lightly barded horse, composite recurve bow, quiver at the hip, straight sword. Keep the silhouette leaner than the Immortals. Dyed reds and ochres are an artistic choice.
enemyRoster.justification: Mounted archery was standard in Sasanian warfare, but no light-cavalry unit at Avarayr is named in the sources I could read.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: The Sasanian army at Avarayr included the elite cavalry corps known as the Immortals (Hewsen in Encyclopaedia Iranica, per the researcher's extract; Wikipedia 'Vardan Mamikonian' and 'Battle of Avarayr'). 'Immortals' is the Greek name used by Roman historians; Armenian sources allude to an elite royal corps whose Persian name and size are debated. Ammianus 25.1.12 (363) describes Persian horsemen covered in close-fitting iron plates with metal face masks, so that arrows could lodge only at the eye-holes and nostrils; 25.1.13 mentions men armed with pikes; 24.6.8 says the horses wore leather coverings.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Rider fully covered in mail and fitted plates, metal face mask with small eye openings, long pike held two-handed, horse in leather barding; dull iron grey with minimal color. Slow, heavy gait. Ammianus describes the Persian army of 363, so this is the closest eyewitness look rather than a 451 detail.
enemyRoster.justification: An elite cavalry corps rendered as the Immortals is attested at Avarayr; the equipment comes from the best late antique eyewitness description of Persian heavy cavalry, 88 years earlier.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: Elephants were part of the Sasanian army at Avarayr and decided the day: the Armenians held their own until the elephant corps was brought up (Hewsen, per the researcher's extract; Wikipedia 'Vardan Mamikonian'). At Amida in 359 Ammianus saw Persian elephants 'loaded with armed men' (19.2.3), and he reports that their drivers carried a knife bound to the right hand to kill a maddened elephant (25.1.15). Kurkjian, paraphrasing Yeghishe, describes elephants carrying iron-clad towers full of bowmen (not re-checked). M. B. Charles, Iranica Antiqua 42 (2007), studies the Sasanian elephant corps.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Asian elephant with a timber tower holding 2-3 archers (iron plating per Kurkjian's paraphrase, treat as optional); driver on the neck with a long knife strapped to his right hand; armored infantry escort jogging alongside. Scale it so the tower rises above tower-defense walls.
enemyRoster.justification: Elephants at Avarayr are in every account consulted. The siege slot matches the era mechanic and their use against Amida's walls in 359; the tower crew is attested for Amida, and for Avarayr only through Kurkjian's paraphrase.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: No aerial combatants appear in any account of Avarayr I consulted. Falconry was a Sasanian royal pursuit: Ferdowsi (c. 1000 AD) describes large falconry retinues of Bahram V and Khosrow II (Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Bazdari', per the researcher's extract).
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Saker falcons or goshawks in brown and grey plumage, leather jesses trailing, released in flights from a falconer at the map edge. Small, fast, low hit points.
enemyRoster.justification: A real Sasanian animal rather than a fantasy creature, but its combat use is invented. Label it as gameplay in any codex text.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: Mushkan Niusalavurt commanded the Sasanian army at Avarayr, appointed by Mihr-Narseh, and survived the battle heavily wounded (Wikipedia 'Mushkan Niusalavurt'). Kurkjian, paraphrasing Yeghishe, says the Persian commandant directed the battle from a barbed tower on an elephant; I could not re-check this.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Largest elephant on the map, tower with a spiked parapet, the commander in mail and a richly dyed coat with an officer's standard, ringed by Immortal clibanarii. Slow, high HP. At 0 HP he withdraws wounded rather than dying, since the real Mushkan survived.
enemyRoster.justification: The commander is attested; that he commanded from an elephant rests on a secondary paraphrase of Yeghishe. Codex text should say 'according to Yeghishe, as retold by Kurkjian'.

towerAudit.reason: Archery was central to late antique Iranian and Armenian aristocratic warfare (Ammianus 25.1.13 on Persian archers; Wikipedia 'Aswaran'). The Armenian army was made of contingents furnished by the princely houses, each under its own prince, with supreme command held by the hereditary sparapet (Adontz, quoted in Wikipedia 'Sparapet'), and its cavalry was the elite arm. No source I could read describes Armenian archers at Avarayr specifically.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: Timber and rubble-stone platform; bowmen in mail shirts or quilted coats with composite bows and hip quivers; plain-colored pennants (house heraldry for 451 is unverified, keep it generic). Avoid kite or heater shields, which are high-medieval forms.

towerAudit.reason: Ammianus (23.4.1-3) describes the ballista of his day, and at Amida in 359 the Persians set a ballista on top of each iron-fronted siege tower (19.5.1, 19.7.2); he does not say these were captured engines. Avarayr was an open-field battle and no account I could read mentions artillery there, so a field bolt-thrower is license. Do not call it 'scorpio': Ammianus says that in his day 'scorpion' meant the stone-thrower now called the onager.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: Low wooden frame with paired torsion springs of twisted cord, a long grooved slider, and an iron-tipped wooden bolt; crewmen on both sides turning the rollers and a gunner aiming from the rear, as in Ammianus 23.4.2.

towerAudit.reason: The one-armed torsion stone-thrower was current: Ammianus (23.4.4-7) says the engine once called scorpion is now called onager, and at Amida in 359 Roman onagers smashed the Persian siege towers (19.7.7). The traction trebuchet reached the eastern Mediterranean only in the late 6th century (Avaro-Slav use at Thessalonica in 586, Byzantine adoption possibly 587, Persian adoption in the early 7th century), and the counterweight trebuchet in the 12th century. So the skin must be an onager, never a trebuchet. No artillery is recorded at Avarayr itself.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: Heavy low timber frame bound with a horizontal skein of twisted rope; a single arm rising from it with a hemp sling on iron hooks; in front, a great hair-cloth cushion stuffed with chaff on a bed of turf or sun-dried brick to stop the arm; four men on each side winding it down and a gunner with a hammer to knock out the release pin (Ammianus 23.4.4-6). No pivoting beam, no counterweight box.

towerAudit.reason: The war of 449-451 was fought against an edict imposing Zoroastrianism. In 450 a fire temple was installed inside Etchmiadzin Cathedral itself (remains found in the 1950s), and the first term of the Treaty of Nvarsak (484) was that existing fire-altars in Armenia be destroyed and no new ones built. A fire altar on the defenders' side reverses the meaning of the conflict; in this era it belongs, if anywhere, on the enemy side of the map.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: Small gabled stone church of tuff blocks with a plain cross, modeled on surviving early Armenian churches such as the Kasagh basilica at Aparan (4th or 5th century); a priest with a censer at the door. Attack: thrown firebrands and lobbed pots of burning oil, keeping the fire-damage role (Ammianus 19.7.7 records firebrands driving back Persian elephants at Amida; the oil pots are game license). No khachkars, which begin in the 9th century.

towerAudit.reason: I found no source for drums in either army at Avarayr. A morale aura fits something that is attested: before the battle the priest Ghevond addressed the army and the soldiers took communion.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: A priest in dark vestments holding a Gospel book aloft on a small rise, deacons with censers and candles, a portable altar table; the aura is drawn as candlelight and incense smoke spreading to nearby towers.

mechanicAudit.existingMechanic: Persian era: war elephants that stun towers.
mechanicAudit.reason: Keep the elephants: they are attested at Avarayr and decided the day (the Armenian line held until they were brought up). Ammianus supports the stun as a terror effect (25.1.14 and 25.3.4: men and horses could hardly endure the elephants' smell, trumpeting and look) and supports fire and stone as counters (19.7.7: at Amida firebrands drove the elephants back and onagers wrecked the siege towers; 25.1.15: drivers carried knives to kill a maddened elephant before it crushed its own side, remembering a disaster at Nisibis). Add the day's other turning point, the defection of the houses led by Vasak, without making the Siwnik troops monsters. The draft's '3,000 men per elephant' figure is dropped from the rationale: I found it in no source I could read.
mechanicAudit.proposal: War Elephant (siege archetype): 900 HP, 25% physical armor, speed 0.6x base. Terror: when its path passes within 60 px of a tower, that tower is stunned for 2.0 s (8 s cooldown per elephant; a tower cannot be re-stunned for 3 s after a stun ends). Escort: enemy infantry within 100 px of a living elephant take 20% less damage. Panic (after Ammianus 19.7.7 and 25.1.15): each Onager hit or Martyrs' Chapel fire hit adds 1 Panic stack; 3 stacks within 4 s make the elephant turn back for 1.5 s, dealing 60 trample damage to enemy units within 40 px, and remove its Escort aura for 6 s. Boss, Mushkan's Command Elephant: 4,000 HP, 30% armor, speed 0.5x; while alive, elephants within 200 px gain +15% speed; at 50% HP it calls the elephant line forward and 2 War Elephants spawn at the path entrance (once per fight). At 0 HP the boss withdraws instead of dying, with the line 'Mushkan, wounded, quits the field'. Optional scripted event, 'The Defection': at the start of wave 6 of 10, up to 2 player towers built on marked 'Siwnik' slots go silent for 12 s; towers inside a Ghevond's Exhortation aura are immune. Tooltip: 'Several noble houses led by Vasak of Siwnik went over to the Persians.'

eras.heroNote: Yes. Vardan Mamikonian (scholarly transliteration Vardan Mamikonean) is the period-correct hero for this era, and this is the only era where he fits: hereditary sparapet, head of the Mamikonian house, leader of the 450-451 revolt, killed at Avarayr in 451 (26 May or 2 June; sources differ). Because he died in the battle, frame the hero's fall and revive as martyrdom (Vardanants) rather than invented survival. For a campaign epilogue or an unlockable second hero, the attested successor is his nephew Vahan Mamikonian (son of Hmayeak), leader of the 481/482-484 revolt, who secured the Treaty of Nvarsak in 484 and was appointed marzpan in 485 (Wikipedia 'Vahan I Mamikonian'; Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Mamikonean Family' per the researcher's extract). Vardan is anachronistic for the Urartian, Arab and Ottoman eras; those need their own heroes.

mapRecommendation.reason: Avarayr was a river plain in the Araxes basin, along the Tghmut (Tłmut, today the Zangmar), which flows past Maku and joins the Araxes at Poldasht (Wikipedia 'Avarayr Plain', 'Zangmar River'; Hewsen in Encyclopaedia Iranica per the researcher's extract). The site is near the village of Churs in West Azerbaijan, Iran. The game's existing Persian-era level already pairs Araxes Crossing with Avarayr. The other maps fit less well: Tushpa Vale is lakeside Van, Gyumri Road is winter, and Lori Gates has monasteries built centuries later.
mapRecommendation.mapAnachronisms: Araxes Crossing: the battle was on the Tghmut tributary, not the Araxes itself; for this level consider 'Banks of the Tghmut' or 'Plain of Avarayr' (canton of Artaz). The date is late May or early June, so a spring-green plain fits better than a golden harvest (local harvest timing unverified). Tushpa Vale: 'Tushpa' is Urartian; by 451 the city was Van and the district Tosp. The province name Vaspurakan is rare in early Armenian historians (first in Movses Khorenatsi, whose date is disputed), so avoid it in 451-era text. Gyumri Road: 'Gyumri' is a modern form, and the claimed Urartian attestation of 'Kumayri' is unverified; for 451 use 'Shirak Road' (Shirak was a Kamsarakan domain, and Arshavir II Kamsarakan, Vardan's son-in-law, joined the 451 revolt). Lori Gates: Lori fortress dates to 1065, Sanahin's first church to the 930s-940s and Haghpat to about 976, so none existed in 451. Use 'Tashir', the canton of Gugark that stayed Armenian when the rest of Gugark passed to Iberia after 387, and swap the monasteries for small early stone churches or remove them. Avoid khachkars on every map in this era (first true examples 9th century; oldest dated 879, Garni).

claims.source: V. Kurkjian, A History of Armenia (1958), ch. 20, per researcher's extract (penelope.uchicago.edu blocked, not re-fetched); secondary paraphrase

claims.claim: Secondary summaries say each elephant at Avarayr had 3,000 supporting men and that elephants served as command posts.

claims.source: Absence from all accounts read (Wikipedia 'Battle of Avarayr', 'Vardan Mamikonian', 'Mushkan Niusalavurt'; Hewsen and Kurkjian extracts)

corrections: dateRange: Draft said scholarship gives 'Pentecost, 2 June 451' and attributed it to Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Yazdegerd II'. By the Alexandrian Easter reckoning Easter 451 was 8 April, so Pentecost was 27 May; 2 June 451 was a Saturday and cannot be Pentecost. The Iranica attribution could not be checked (site blocked). Current Wikipedia articles ('Battle of Avarayr', 'Vardan Mamikonian', 'Yazdegerd II', 'Mihr-Narseh') give 2 June without the Pentecost label; Wikipedia 'Churs', 'Vahan I Mamikonian' and Kurkjian give 26 May. Both are now reported as variants and no consensus is claimed.
dateline: Draft gave '26 May 451 AD' as if certain; changed to 'spring 451 AD', which is true under either date.

Mushkan's role: Draft said he was 'leading the elite corps called the Immortals'. Per Wikipedia 'Mushkan Niusalavurt', Mihr-Narseh made him head of all the Iranian forces; the Immortals were one corps in his army. Added that he survived the battle heavily wounded. The briefing now reads 'the King's general, Mushkan Niusalavurt, comes with the armored horsemen of the Immortals and a corps of war elephants'.
Vasak Siwni: Draft said he 'died in 452 at Ctesiphon'. The place appears in no source I could read (Wikipedia 'Vasak Siwni' gives only d. 452 after imprisonment); 'at Ctesiphon' removed.
Yazdegerd II: Draft gave his reign as 439-457. Wikipedia 'Yazdegerd II' gives 438-457, while Wikipedia 'Vardan Mamikonian' puts his accession in 439; now given as 438 or 439 to 457.

Vahan's war: Draft said Vahan beat a Persian army at Nersehapat 'in spring 484'. Wikipedia 'Vahan I Mamikonian' puts Nersehapat (in Artaz) in early 483, before the defeat at Akesga and before Peroz's death in 484. Now 482/483, moderate confidence.

Ballista tower: Draft said 'Sasanians mounted captured ballistae on siege towers at Amida in 359'. Ammianus 19.5.1 and 19.7.2 (Rolfe translation, read directly) say a ballista stood on top of each Persian iron-fronted tower, but a full-text search finds nothing about them being captured. 'Captured' removed.

Ballista reskin: Draft named it 'Scorpio Bolt-Thrower'. Ammianus 23.4.4 and 23.4.7 say that in his day 'scorpion' meant the one-armed stone-thrower now called the onager, so the name would collide with the Catapult slot. Renamed 'Field Ballista'. 'Twisted-sinew' changed to 'twisted cord' and 'two crewmen' to crewmen 'on both sides' at the rollers, as in Ammianus 23.4.2.

Briefing: Draft said 'Armenia's bishops and princes refused'. Per Wikipedia 'Vardan Mamikonian', the 449 Artashat assembly declared loyalty to both the Sasanian state and the Christian faith; the magnates were then forced to convert at Ctesiphon, renounced the conversion on returning home, and rebelled in 450. The briefing now says this, which is accurate and still heroic.

Briefing: Draft said Ghevond 'gave the army communion and baptized those not yet received into the Church'. The communion is supported (Wikipedia 'Battle of Avarayr'). The baptism detail rests only on the researcher's extract of an Armenian Church web page, which I could not re-open. The briefing now says Ghevond spoke to the army and the soldiers received communion; the baptism appears only as a low-confidence part of a claim.
Briefing length and tone: rewritten body is 248 words (within 170-260), keeps the heroic rally, states the defeat plainly, and makes no victory claims.

Boss accuracy: Draft labeled 'Mushkan Niusalavurt's Command Elephant' as 'attested' although its own justification rated the elephant-borne command as moderate. The commander is attested; that he rode an elephant rests on Kurkjian's paraphrase, which I could not re-check. Downgraded to 'plausible'. Since Mushkan survived wounded, the boss now withdraws at 0 HP instead of dying.

Mechanic audit: Draft's rationale cited 'each elephant 3,000 supporting men' (low confidence). I found this in no source I could read, so it is removed from the design rationale and kept only as a low-confidence claim.

Mechanic audit: Draft labeled the fire and stone counterplay 'game license, not sourced'. Ammianus 19.7.7 records Roman onagers wrecking Persian siege towers and firebrands driving the elephants back at Amida, and 25.1.15 records drivers carrying knives to kill maddened elephants that might crush their own side. The counterplay now cites these passages and adds a trample-own-escort effect.

Fire Altar audit: Draft said 'The rebels destroyed fire-altars'. I found no support for this in the sources I could read, so it is removed. It is replaced with the Etchmiadzin evidence (Wikipedia 'Etchmiadzin Cathedral': a fire temple installed inside the cathedral in 450) and the first Nvarsak term.

Martyrs' Chapel visual: Draft said 'small gabled single-nave chapel ... like the Kasagh basilica'. Kasagh is a basilica, not a single-nave chapel, and the 'dark grey tuff' detail is unverified. Reworded. The fire attack now rests on firebrands (Ammianus 19.7.7), with oil pots marked as license.

Flyer: Draft said no aerial combatants are recorded 'in any late antique battle'. That sweeping negative cannot be verified and is not needed, so the claim is limited to the Avarayr accounts consulted.

Spearmen: Draft cited pay 'graded separately from cavalry' (not verifiable by me) and a 'simple iron helmet'. Wikipedia 'Paygan' describes conscript infantry with light wooden or wicker shields, leather caps and short spears. The visual is updated and the pay detail dropped.
Heavy cavalry: added that 'Immortals' is a Greek/Roman label whose Persian name and size are debated (Wikipedia 'Immortals (Sasanian Empire)'), and added leather horse coverings from Ammianus 24.6.8.
Elephant visual: Draft gave the mahout a goad. Ammianus 25.1.15 says Persian drivers carried a knife bound to the right hand; changed to match.
Leontine martyrs: Draft gave 454/455. Wikipedia 'Leontine martyrs' gives 455; now given as 455 with 454 as a variant.

Catholicos Hovsep: Draft said he 'headed the bishops who rejected the conversion edict at Artashat'. Wikipedia 'Vardan Mamikonian' describes the 449 Artashat assembly as nobles and clergy (marzpan Vasak, Vardan, the bdeashkh of Gugark and the acting Catholicos) declaring loyalty to the state and to their faith. Reworded.

Marcian: added that the 450 embassy, led by Hmayeak Mamikonian, first reached Theodosius II, who received it favorably but died; Marcian then refused on the advice of Anatolius and Florentius (Wikipedia 'Marcian').
Treaty of Nvarsak: Draft listed three terms. Wikipedia 'Treaty of Nvarsak' and 'Balash' add a fourth: the king to govern Armenia in person, not through deputies. Added.
Vardanants: Draft said 'Thursday before Great Lent'. Wikipedia 'Vardan Mamikonian' specifies the last Thursday before Great Lent.

Traction trebuchet: Draft said it reached the Byzantine-Avar world around 587. Refined per Wikipedia 'Mangonel': Avaro-Slav use at Thessalonica in 586, Byzantine adoption possibly by 587, Persian adoption in the early 7th century.

Map anachronisms: Draft said Kumayri is 'securely attested only in medieval sources (a 773 context)'. I could not verify the 773 detail, and Wikipedia 'Gyumri' asserts an Urartian attestation that I could not check either. Simplified to: 'Gyumri' is modern, the age of 'Kumayri' is disputed, use 'Shirak'. Also flagged that 'Vaspurakan' as a province name is rare in early Armenian historians (Wikipedia 'Vaspurakan').

Map anachronisms: dates made precise (Sanahin's first church 930s-940s and Holy Savior 966; Haghpat probably 976). Added that Tashir alone of Gugark stayed Armenian after 387 (Wikipedia 'Gugark') and that Arshavir II Kamsarakan of Shirak was Vardan's son-in-law.
Era and dateRange: Draft gave the revolt as 449-451. The edict and the Artashat assembly were in 449 and the armed revolt in 450-451 (Wikipedia 'Vardan Mamikonian'); made explicit.

Casualty figures (1,036 Armenians, 3,544 Persians) and the 'death understood' quotation are kept only as Yeghishe's words, at moderate confidence. They do not appear in the 2023 Wikipedia texts I read, and I could not re-open the Iranica and Church pages the researcher cited.
Removed the Dailamite infantry and Amida 502-503 claims from the claims list, since nothing in the dossier now depends on them.

Verification method: the WebSearch budget was used up, and Iranica, Wikipedia, Perseus, Lacus Curtius and most other sites were blocked by the egress proxy. I checked against (a) Ammianus, Rolfe translation, Perseus TEI text from GitHub, read directly, and (b) the full English Wikipedia text of 1 June 2023 from the TensorFlow Datasets mirror. Claims that rest only on the draft researcher's search extracts say so in their source field.

eras.era: Era 3: The Arab invasions of Armenia, 640-655 AD (Rashidun Caliphate under the caliphs Umar and Uthman, with Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan as governor of Syria; Byzantine emperor Constans II, r. 641-668)
eras.dateRange: 640: first Arab raid reaches Dvin; the history attributed to Sebeos and Catholicos John V date its fall to 640, and Encyclopaedia Iranica gives 6 October 640 (a Friday in the Julian calendar). Variants: 641 in some Armenian survey histories, 642 in older scholarship (Lynch 1901) and in Wikipedia's 'Arminiya', and a separate storming on 6 January 642 in Wikipedia's 'Dvin'. 643: second invasion ravages Ayrarat and is defeated by Theodoros Rshtuni. 650: three-year Arab-Byzantine truce negotiated in Damascus. 652 or 653 (sources split): Theodoros accepts Mu'awiya's overlordship by treaty. 653-654: Constans II in Armenia in person, wintering at Dvin (the winter is given as 652-653 or 653-654) and leaving in spring 654. 654-655: Arab campaign under Habib ibn Maslama; Theodosiopolis (Qaliqala) taken in 655; Theodoros taken to Syria and dies there in 655 or 656. 656-657: Arab authority lapses during the First Fitna and Hamazasp Mamikonian returns to Byzantine allegiance; 661: the princes re-submit to Mu'awiya. Muslim sources compress the conquest into one campaign of 645/646.

briefing.title: The Lord of Rshtunik
briefing.body:
In 640 the armies of the caliphate reached Dvin, the capital of Armenia. The history attributed to Bishop Sebeos, written by a man who lived through those years, says the attackers drove the defenders from the walls with smoke and arrows, raised their ladders, and led away 35,000 captives.

Now, in 643, they have come again. An Arab army is ravaging the plain of Ayrarat, and one of its columns has fallen on the fortress of Artsap in Kogovit. Riding to meet it is Theodoros Rshtuni, lord of Rshtunik on the southern shore of Lake Van, commander of the Armenian forces and patrician of the empire. On the same plain, Catholicos Nerses III is raising the great round church of Zvartnots, a promise in stone that Armenia means to endure.

Know the road ahead. Theodoros will win this fight, and Emperor Constans II will recognize him as ruler of Armenia. Within ten years, with new invasions looming, he will make terms with Muawiya, governor of Syria: Armenia keeps 15,000 horsemen of its own, and no Arab emir enters its fortresses. He will die in Syria, and Armenia will pass under the caliphate, yet its church and its princely houses will endure.

Dvin fell. At Artsap, Theodoros answered. Answer with him. Man the walls, keep the archers supplied, and let no ladder touch the stone. Commander, Ayrarat is yours to hold.
briefing.stakes: Relieve the fortress of Artsap and hold the plain of Ayrarat against the Arab raid of 643, so its people are not carried off as Dvin's were in 640.
briefing.victoryEpilogue: Theodoros Rshtuni's victory of 643 was real, and Constans II recognized him as ruler of Armenia. It bought a decade, not lasting freedom: in 652 or 653 Theodoros accepted Muawiya's overlordship on terms that kept Armenia's own cavalry and kept Arab garrisons out, and in 654-655 Habib ibn Maslama's campaign took Theodosiopolis while Theodoros was carried off to Syria, where he died. Armenia passed under the caliphate, yet its church and its princely houses endured, and Theodoros was brought home to be buried in Rshtunik.
briefing.defeatEpilogue: The column breaks through, as the raiders of 640 broke through at Dvin, and the plain is stripped of its people. History went better than this: in 643 Theodoros Rshtuni turned the raid back. Rally the princes and try again.
didYouKnow: The history attributed to Bishop Sebeos says the Arabs who took Dvin in 640 cleared its walls with smoke and arrows, scaled them with ladders, and led away 35,000 captives.
Under the pact of 652 or 653, Muawiya promised no tribute for three years, let Armenia keep 15,000 cavalry of its own, and pledged to send no emir into Armenian fortresses.

Zvartnots Cathedral was begun in the 640s under Catholicos Nerses III, in the very years of the first Arab raids, and since 2000 has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage site with the churches of Etchmiadzin.
Al-Baladhuri preserves Habib ibn Maslama's guarantee to the Christians, Magians and Jews of Dvin, protecting their lives, property, churches, synagogues and city wall in return for jizya and kharaj.
The Rshtuni princes ruled Rshtunik on the southern shore of Lake Van, and Theodoros used the island of Aghtamar as his seat and refuge.
Manuk Abeghian and other scholars saw the memory of Theodoros Rshtuni in Uncle Toros (K'eri T'oros) of the Armenian epic of David of Sasun.

keyFigures.name: Theodoros Rshtuni (T'eodoros Rshtuni; Theodore Rshtuni)
keyFigures.role: Lord of Rshtunik; sparapet (commander-in-chief) of the Armenian forces; presiding prince of Armenia; Byzantine patrikios
keyFigures.side: Armenian (Byzantine-aligned until 652/653, then under Arab overlordship)
keyFigures.note: Born c. 590 (Wikipedia). Became leading prince after David Saharuni was overthrown (638 or 640). Fought the 640 raid alongside the Byzantine general Procopius, when a failed maneuver let the Arabs reach Dvin. Made commander-in-chief and patrikios by Constans II in 641 on the advice of Catholicos Nerses III. In 643 defeated the Arab invasion of Ayrarat; Armenian accounts place the decisive fight at the relief of the fortress of Artsap in Kogovit (the figure of about 3,000 Arabs is low confidence). Recognized as ruler of Armenia by Constans II, though he was also blamed for the defeat of a Byzantine army under Procopius (an Armenian survey adds that Constans briefly arrested him). Accepted Mu'awiya's overlordship in 652 or 653. Taken to Syria in 654 or 655 and died there in 655 or 656; his body was brought back and buried in Rshtunik.

keyFigures.name: Constans II
keyFigures.role: Byzantine emperor (r. 641-668)
keyFigures.note: Campaigned in Armenia in person after Theodoros's submission to the Arabs, reportedly with 100,000 men (a chronicle figure), wintered at Dvin and left in spring 654; the winter is given as 652-653 in one Wikipedia article and 653-654 in others. Sebeos is reported to describe a communion scene with him at Dvin (not re-verified). Tried to impose Chalcedonian doctrine on the Armenians.

keyFigures.name: Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan (Muawiya)
keyFigures.role: Governor of Syria under Caliph Uthman; caliph from 661
keyFigures.note: Negotiated a three-year truce with the Byzantine envoy Procopios in Damascus in 650; received Theodoros Rshtuni's submission in 652 or 653 (terms preserved in Sebeos); Theodoros came to him with gifts. Habib ibn Maslama campaigned in Armenia under his command.

keyFigures.name: Habib ibn Maslama al-Fihri
keyFigures.role: Arab general; briefly governor of the conquered Armenian territories, later governor of Armenia and Adharbayjan
keyFigures.note: Born in Mecca in the 610s, died c. 662 (one account has him alive in 671). Led a cavalry squadron at Yarmuk; nicknamed Habib al-Rum. Took Theodosiopolis (Qaliqala), defeated the Byzantine general Maurianos, received the submission of princes around Lake Van, and took Dvin and Tiflis by capitulation; the treaties are preserved, Dvin's by al-Baladhuri. Muslim sources place the campaign right after Uthman's accession (644), i.e. 645/646; Byzantine and Armenian sources place it about ten years later (653/654-655).

keyFigures.name: Nerses III Tayetsi, 'the Builder' (Nerses Shinogh / Shinarar)
keyFigures.role: Catholicos of All Armenians (641-661; some lists 640-661)
keyFigures.note: Advised Constans II to give Theodoros command in 641. Presided over the building of Zvartnots near Vagharshapat, begun in the 640s (643 in most accounts) and consecrated by 652 according to Movses Kaghankatvatsi (not re-verified). Pro-Byzantine; resided in exile in Tayk c. 653-658. Reported to have moved the patriarchal residence from Dvin to Zvartnots after the Arab occupation of Dvin (not re-verified).

keyFigures.name: Hamazasp Mamikonian (numbered Hamazasp II or IV in different lists)
keyFigures.role: Presiding prince of Armenia from 655
keyFigures.side: Armenian (installed under the Arabs, returned to Byzantine allegiance during the First Fitna)
keyFigures.note: From the house of Vardan Mamikonian. Installed in 655 after Theodoros's removal; English Wikipedia's 'Theodore Rshtuni' calls him Theodoros's son-in-law, while 'Arminiya' calls him a rival. Returned to Byzantine overlordship when Arab authority lapsed in 656-657 and was reportedly made curopalates by Constans II (not re-verified). End of rule given as 658 (English Wikipedia lists) or 661 (Armenian Wikipedia).

keyFigures.name: Sebeos
keyFigures.role: Armenian bishop and historian
keyFigures.note: A 'Bishop Sebeos of the Bagratunis' signed the acts of the Council of Dvin in 645; the history is published as 'The Armenian History attributed to Sebeos' (trans. R. W. Thomson, commentary J. Howard-Johnston, 1999). It is a contemporary account and the principal source for 640-655; modern historians prefer it, partly corroborated by Theophanes, over the Arabic sources.

keyFigures.name: Procopius (Byzantine general, 640s)
keyFigures.role: Byzantine commander in Armenia
keyFigures.note: Named as Theodoros's colleague against the 640 raid, and as commander of a Byzantine army defeated around 643 for which Theodoros was blamed. A Byzantine envoy named Procopios negotiated the 650 truce in Damascus; whether he is the same man is unverified. Not the 6th-century historian of the same name.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: Rashidun armies were divided into infantry and light cavalry; in their usual tactic the infantry and archers engaged and held the enemy while the cavalry was kept back to strike the flanks. Camels carried men and supplies on long marches (Wikipedia, 'Rashidun Caliphate').
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Foot soldier with long spear and round shield, sword on a shoulder baldric; head-cloth wrapped over a cap or simple helmet; undyed wool or linen tunic, mostly unarmoured, a few with mail shirts. Palette: cream, sand, brown, dull indigo. Optional: wave enters riding camels in file and dismounts at a marked line. Gear details follow Nicolle, Armies of Islam 7th-11th Centuries (Osprey), cited by the researcher but not text-verified.
enemyRoster.justification: Infantry spearmen and archers are attested for early Muslim armies in general; no source located gives the infantry share of the 640 or 643 raids into Armenia. The camel-to-foot hook is plausible license, not a documented tactic in these raids: camel-mounted (speed x1.6) until 40% of the path, then dismount (normal speed, +10% HP).

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: Cavalry was the main strike force and mobile reserve of Rashidun armies (Wikipedia, 'Rashidun Caliphate'); Habib ibn Maslama himself had led a cavalry squadron at Yarmuk. The 640 and 643 incursions ravaged Ayrarat and carried off captives (Sebeos as summarized in Wikipedia).
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Light horseman on a small, fine-boned horse, long lance and sword, round shield on the back, head-cloth trailing; little or no horse armour. Fast, low silhouette, dust trail.
enemyRoster.justification: Horsemen are attested in Rashidun armies, and raiding cavalry fits the speed and reach of the 640 and 643 raids, but the sources located give no cavalry figures for these Armenian raids.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: The mubarizun were champions in early Muslim armies whose role was to meet enemy champions in single combat before the general advance (Wikipedia, 'Mubarizun', per the researcher); duels between leading fighters opened the battle of Siffin in 657 (Wikipedia, 'Mu'awiya I').
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Big infantry silhouette in a knee-length mail coat over a tunic, iron helmet with head-cloth wound around it, sword and round shield, sometimes a mace. Slow, deliberate stride. Darker, richer cloth than the rank and file.
enemyRoster.justification: The champion role is attested; equipping them as heavily armoured is a reasonable reading, not documented for Armenia. Gameplay hook: 'Challenge' makes it target the hero first if within 3 tiles (duel), taking 30% less damage from the hero while dueling.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: The history attributed to Sebeos, on Dvin in 640: the attackers drove the defenders from the ramparts with smoke and arrows, then set up ladders, scaled the walls, and entered the city.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Four-man team: two carry a long wooden scaling ladder, one carries a smoking brazier or bundle of burning brushwood, one archer escorts. Grey smoke plume trailing. No wheeled engines.
enemyRoster.justification: The best-attested assault technique of this era in Armenia, and it drives the replacement for the sandstorm mechanic. Arabs were using traction trebuchets by the 650s (siege of Dongola, 652), but no source located shows them in Armenia 640-655, so the unit carries no engine.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: No flying units existed. Least-bad option: light skirmishers taking mountain tracks above the road, bypassing the valley path; only ranged towers can reach them on the heights.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Lightly clad men with bows or javelins, rope coils, bare forearms, moving along cliff edges on an elevated render layer with a drop shadow on the ground below. No wings, no animals.
enemyRoster.justification: Keeps the anti-air rule (direct-line pathing, only Archers and Ballista can hit) without fantasy creatures. Rejected alternatives: war falcons (falconry is hunting, not combat) and fire-arrow 'units' (projectiles, not soldiers). No specific 7th-century episode of cliff infiltration in Armenia was located: unverified.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: Arab general (born in Mecca in the 610s, died c. 662) under Mu'awiya who took Theodosiopolis, defeated the Byzantine general Maurianos, received the submission of the Lake Van princes, took Dvin by capitulation, and was appointed governor of the subdued Armenian territories (Wikipedia, 'Habib ibn Maslama al-Fihri'; al-Baladhuri).
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Mounted commander in a long mail coat and helmet wrapped with a head-cloth, sword and lance, escorted by a banner-bearer and two mubariz guards. Avoid inventing specific banner colours or inscriptions (not verified).
enemyRoster.justification: Real commander of the decisive campaign. His capture of Dvin was by treaty, not a massacre, and its date is disputed (right after 644 in Muslim sources, 653/654-655 in Armenian and Byzantine ones), so a boss appearance in a 643 level is game license; place him as the 'final wave' foreshadowing the 650s.

towerAudit.reason: Archery is central to the sources for this era: Sebeos says arrows (with smoke) cleared Dvin's walls in 640, Rashidun tactics used infantry and archers to hold the enemy, and the Strategikon describes bow-armed Byzantine cavalry. Armenian forces were raised by noble houses: each nakharar had his own army.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: Retainers of a noble house on a stone parapet: conical iron helmets, mail or quilted coats, composite recurved bows, quivers at the hip. Do not invent Rshtuni heraldry; plain cloth pennants only. Specific Armenian archer kit not text-verified.

towerAudit.reason: Procopius describes Belisarius placing ballistae on the towers of Rome in 537-538, and Byzantine forces operated in Armenia in the 640s-650s. But the traction trebuchet had largely displaced torsion engines in the eastern Mediterranean by the late 6th century, Dennis argues the Strategikon's 'ballista' may already mean traction artillery, and no source located shows a ballista in Armenian defence 640-655.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: Two-armed frame engine on a wall platform, iron-tipped bolts, crew of two in Byzantine-style tunics and helmets. Keep it fixed on walls, no wheeled field carriage.

towerAudit.reason: The traction trebuchet reached the eastern Mediterranean with the Avars (Avaro-Slav attack on Thessalonica in 586, per the Miracles of St Demetrius) and was adopted by the Byzantines possibly from 587, the Persians in the early 7th century and the Arabs in the second half of the 7th century. A generic torsion 'catapult' is dated for this era; a traction trebuchet is the correct form. No use in Armenia 640-655 specifically was located.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: Pivoting beam on a timber trestle, sling at the long arm, 6-10 men hauling ropes at the short arm; rough stone shot. Fires with a visible crew pull animation.

towerAudit.reason: A fire altar is a Zoroastrian (Sasanian Persian) religious installation. 7th-century Armenia was Christian, its Catholicos building Zvartnots; an Armenian fire-altar tower misrepresents the defenders, and contradicts the 451 era's own theme of resisting imposed Zoroastrianism.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: Crew at a parapet brazier lobbing clay pots with cloth wicks, filled with sulphur, pitch and naphtha, as the defenders of Petra in Lazica did against Byzantine siege engines in 550-551 (Procopius). Orange burning patch on the path (damage-over-time zone), black smoke. Do not label it Greek fire, first used at the Arab siege of Constantinople in the 670s.

towerAudit.reason: A command/morale aura is a reasonable abstraction, but no source located documents war drums in 7th-century Armenian armies, or Arab use of war drums in these specific campaigns: unverified. Renaming avoids asserting an unattested instrument.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: Raised wooden platform with a standard-bearer and two horn-blowers; plain banner with a cross finial (artistic license, not a documented Rshtuni standard). Aura ring pulses with each horn blast.

mechanicAudit.existingMechanic: Sandstorm: periodic weather that reduces tower range/visibility.
mechanicAudit.reason: The Armenian highlands are not desert, and no source located describes sandstorms in any Armenian campaign; a sandstorm also implies the invaders 'brought the desert' with them, a stereotype rather than history. The era's best-attested battlefield detail is Sebeos's account of Dvin (640): smoke and arrows drove defenders off the walls before ladders went up, which maps directly onto a range/visibility debuff. Armenian sources also record winter cold destroying an Arab force, but that account (Ghevond, Vardanakert, winter of 703) is 8th-century; no 7th-century source describing Arab armies harmed by snow in Armenia was located (unverified), so cold is offered as a secondary, clearly labelled weather rule.
mechanicAudit.proposal: 1) SMOKE AND ARROWS (core era mechanic, replaces Sandstorm). Each Smoke-and-Ladder Party lights a smoke pot when within 3 tiles of any tower: cloud radius 2.5 tiles, duration 8 s, cooldown 18 s per unit; a tower can be covered by at most 2 clouds (penalties do not stack beyond the first). Towers inside a cloud: range -25%, fire rate -15%. The Banner and Horns aura halves both penalties. Casting Frost on a cloud disperses it instantly. A ladder party that reaches the exit costs 2 lives instead of 1. Tooltip: 'At Dvin in 640, the history attributed to Sebeos says, the attackers cleared the walls with smoke and arrows, then climbed with ladders.' 2) HIGHLAND COLD (optional weather; on by default for the winter map). Every 90 s, a 15 s cold snap: all enemies -20% speed (horse raiders and the boss -30%), tower range -10% from blowing snow, Frost spell duration +50% during the snap. On Araxes Crossing, ford tiles freeze during a snap; enemies on the ford during its final 3 s take +15% damage ('thin ice'). Tooltip must date the inspiration correctly: 'In the winter of 703, Ghevond writes, Arabs fleeing the Armenians at Vardanakert crossed the frozen Arax; the ice gave way.'

eras.heroNote: Vardan Mamikonian is not appropriate: he fell at Avarayr in 451 (2 June 451 per Wikipedia), about 190 years before this era. Period-correct hero: Theodoros Rshtuni (T'eodoros Rshtuni), lord of Rshtunik on the southern shore of Lake Van, sparapet of the Armenian forces, presiding prince of Armenia and Byzantine patrikios (command and title conferred by Constans II in 641); born c. 590, active 638/640-655, taken to Syria in 654 or 655 and died there in 655 or 656, buried in Rshtunik. Sources: English Wikipedia 'Theodore Rshtuni', 'Arminiya', 'Muslim conquest of Armenia', 'Mu'awiya I' (2023 text, read offline); Armenian Wikipedia 'Hayastane vagh mijnadarum' (Armenia in the early Middle Ages); Sebeos (Bedrosian and Thomson/Howard-Johnston translations, via the researcher's search excerpts). Framing caveat: in 652 or 653 he accepted Mu'awiya's overlordship to spare Armenia a new invasion while keeping 15,000 Armenian cavalry and no Arab garrisons in its fortresses; present this truthfully as strategic survival, not betrayal or triumph. Hero kit idea: 'Lord of Aghtamar' (he used the island of Aghtamar as his seat and refuge). Heroic hook that stays true: some scholars, following Manuk Abeghian, see his memory in Uncle Toros (K'eri T'oros) of the David of Sasun epic. Alternative if the designers want to keep the Mamikonian line: Hamazasp Mamikonian (presiding prince from 655, end date given as 658 or 661), but he is not documented as a battlefield defender against the Arabs, so Theodoros is the stronger choice.

mapRecommendation.reason: Dvin, the capital that fell in 640, lay about 35 km south of modern Yerevan near ancient Artaxata, on the Ararat plain in the Araxes basin; the 643 invasion ravaged Ayrarat; and Zvartnots was rising on the same plain near Vagharshapat from the 640s. The golden-harvest palette also matches the autumn date Iranica gives for Dvin's fall (6 October 640, moderate confidence). The river ford supports the optional 'thin ice' cold-snap rule (Ghevond's 703 Arax ice, labelled as later). Strong alternative: Tushpa Vale for a Theodoros home-defence level (Rshtunik on Lake Van's south shore, Aghtamar island), but that map is tied to the Era 1 Urartian framing.
mapRecommendation.mapAnachronisms: Tushpa Vale: 'Tushpa' is the Urartian capital on the east shore of Lake Van, right for Era 1 only. Its Armenian form Tosp is attested (Movses Khorenatsi calls the city Tosp; Tosp was a district of Vaspurakan), so a 7th-century reskin should use Tosp, Rshtunik (south shore) and Aghtamar island. Gyumri Road: 'Gyumri' is the modern name (chosen 1992); the medieval name Kumayri appears in Ghevond's 8th-century narrative; for 640-655 call it the Shirak road or Kumayri road. The claim that 'Kumayri' appears in Urartian inscriptions is low confidence (no inscription identified). Lori Gates: Lori fortress was built in the 11th century (capital of the Tashir-Dzoraget kingdom from 1065), Sanahin was founded in the 10th century and Haghpat probably in 976, so monasteries there are about 300 years too late. In the 7th century the area was the Tashir canton of Gugark, a province contested between Armenian and Iberian (Georgian) lords; rename 'Tashir Gates' and swap the monasteries for the Odzun domed basilica (dated variously 5th-7th century) or a Zvartnots-style central-plan church. Araxes Crossing: 'Araxes' is the classical Greek form (Armenian Yeraskh, modern Arax); add Zvartnots under construction (scaffolding) for a 643 setting and the walled city of Dvin on the skyline.
