corrections: Draft dateRange and claims paired 17 Shawwal 19 AH with 6 October 640; tabular Hijri conversion gives 10 October 640, so the Hijri equivalent is dropped. The 6 October 640 date is kept at moderate confidence (Iranica excerpt, not re-fetched); it fell on a Friday (computed).

Draft gave only 640 and a '6 January 642' variant for Dvin; added the other circulating dates: 641 (Armenian Wikipedia 'Hayastane vagh mijnadarum'), 642 (English Wikipedia 'Arminiya' and 'Muslim conquest of Armenia'; Lynch 1901). 640 kept as the date of Sebeos and John V per Wikipedia 'Dvin (ancient city)'.

Draft claim that a variant account has the Arabs 'killing 12,000' at Dvin: removed. The 2023 text of Wikipedia 'Dvin (ancient city)' says only 'with many deaths', and no primary source for 12,000 was identified.

Briefing said 'At Artsap, history held': removed. The sources located say Theodoros's army came to the relief of Artsap and crushed the Arab force (Armenian Wikipedia) and that he defeated the Arabs and forced them back (English Wikipedia); none says the fortress itself held. Replaced with 'At Artsap, Theodoros answered.'

Artsap episode date: draft gave it as 643 at moderate confidence with no caveat. Armenian Wikipedia 'Hayastane vagh mijnadarum' places the relief of Artsap 'a few years' after 643; summaries of Sebeos (arak29, Tecimer) place it in 643. Kept as 643, flagged as disputed; the 'c. 3,000 Arabs' figure downgraded to low.

Briefing said 'The bishop Sebeos, who lived through these years, wrote': changed to 'The history attributed to Bishop Sebeos, written by a man who lived through those years', since the work is published as 'The Armenian History attributed to Sebeos' (Thomson/Howard-Johnston 1999) and its authorship is attributed.

Pact date: draft fixed it at 652 ('some reconstructions 653'). English Wikipedia 'Theodore Rshtuni', 'Arminiya' and 'Mu'awiya I' give 653; Armenian Wikipedia and Jinbashian give 652; one chronology gives 651/652. Now '652 or 653' in briefing, epilogue, didYouKnow and claims, confidence moderate.

Victory epilogue said 'Armenia became the caliphate's province of Arminiya' right after 655: overstated. Arab authority lapsed in the First Fitna (656-657), Hamazasp returned to Byzantine allegiance, the princes re-submitted only in 661, and direct provincial rule came after 700 (Wikipedia 'Arminiya'). Reworded to 'Armenia passed under the caliphate'.

Victory epilogue said 'by 654-655 Arab armies under Habib ibn Maslama held Theodosiopolis and Dvin': Dvin's capitulation to Habib is dated 645/646 by Muslim sources and its date in the Armenian chronology is not fixed in the sources located; epilogue now names only Theodosiopolis (655, Wikipedia 'Mu'awiya I').

Hamazasp: draft said 'Hamazasp IV Mamikonian, presiding prince 655-661'. Sources disagree: English Wikipedia lists give 655-658 and number him Hamazasp II; Armenian Wikipedia gives 654-661. 'Theodore Rshtuni' calls him Theodoros's son-in-law while 'Arminiya' calls him a rival. Key figure rewritten with the variants; 'Sebeos praises him as a lover of reading and study' removed (not verifiable).

Draft didYouKnow and claims said Lake Van was 'also called the Sea of Rshtunik': no source located supports this; the attested medieval Armenian name is Bznunyats tsov, Sea of Bznunik (Armenian Wikipedia; English Wikipedia 'Bznuni'). Removed; didYouKnow now uses the Aghtamar seat/refuge, which is sourced.

Draft placed Dvin 'on the left bank of the Azat'; English Wikipedia 'Dvin (ancient city)' places it 'along the banks of the Metsamor River'. River detail removed; '35 km south of Yerevan' kept. Draft's 'Catholicos's seat until the earthquake of 893' removed as unverified (Lynch 1901 gives the transfer of the see to Dvin in 452 but not its end there).

Spearmen basis: draft said early Muslim armies were 'infantry-first' with cavalry as a reserve. Wikipedia 'Rashidun Caliphate' states the cavalry was the main strike force and mobile reserve, with infantry and archers holding the enemy, and camels used for transport. Basis rewritten, unit renamed 'Arab Foot Spearmen', and the camel-dismount hook relabelled as plausible license (low-confidence claim).

Draft claim that 'Arabic manjaniq derives from Greek manganikon, a term first used of Avar machines at Constantinople in 626' removed: not found in the sources available (Wikipedia 'Trebuchet' and 'Mangonel' do not state it).

Trebuchet chronology made precise: the Avaro-Slav attack on Thessalonica is dated 586 (Miracles of St Demetrius); Arabs adopted the traction trebuchet in the second half of the 7th century and used it at Dongola in 652 (Wikipedia 'Trebuchet'). Siege-unit justification updated from the vaguer 'known to the Arabs by this period'.

Ballista audit: added that traction trebuchets had largely displaced torsion engines in the eastern Mediterranean by the late 6th century (Wikipedia 'Trebuchet', 'Torsion siege engine'), which strengthens the acceptable-license verdict. Archers audit: replaced the unverified 'massed archery at Rome' with verified support (Rashidun infantry and archers; Strategikon bow-armed cavalry; each nakharar had his own army).

Map anachronisms: draft marked the Armenian form 'Tosp' unverified. Verified: Movses Khorenatsi calls Van 'Tosp' and Tosp was a district of Vaspurakan (Wikipedia 'Van, Turkey', 'Tosb'). Also noted that Tushpa/Van is on the east side of Lake Van, while Rshtunik is the south shore.

Map anachronisms: added that 7th-century Tashir/Gugark was a contested Armenian-Iberian borderland (Wikipedia 'Tashir (historical region)', 'Gugark'), relevant to a 'Tashir Gates' reskin. Armenian form of Araxes given as Yeraskh (historical) and Arax (modern) per Wikipedia 'Aras (river)', replacing 'Erasx'.

Haghpat/Sanahin UNESCO: draft said both were inscribed in 1996. English Wikipedia says so, but the UNESCO record could not be checked (an extension date for Sanahin may apply); reworded to 'together form a UNESCO site; Haghpat listed 1996'.

Mechanic tooltip: draft gave 'January 703' for Vardanakert; the offline Armenian source gives 'winter of 703' and the January date rests only on the researcher's excerpt. Tooltip now says 'winter of 703'.

Theodoros key figure: added that he was blamed for the defeat of Procopius's Byzantine army (English Wikipedia) and briefly arrested by Constans (Armenian Wikipedia, single source), his 641 appointment on Nerses III's advice, and his burial in Rshtunik. Constans II: added the reported 100,000-man army as a chronicle figure and the 652-653 vs 653-654 winter variant.

Mu'awiya key figure: added the 650 three-year truce negotiated in Damascus with the Byzantine envoy Procopios (Wikipedia 'Mu'awiya I'); Procopius key figure notes the possible but unverified identity with the 640 general.

Nerses III: dates added as 641-661 (some lists 640-661) and his exile in Tayk c. 653-658 added (Wikipedia 'Bana cathedral'); 'begun in 643' kept at moderate since the Zvartnots article was not re-checkable; didYouKnow now says 'begun in the 640s'.

Confidence upgrades: Vardan's death at Avarayr in 451 verified (Wikipedia 'Vardan Mamikonian', 'Battle of Avarayr'); Greek fire upgraded from low to moderate (first use 677/678, Wikipedia 'List of naval battles').

Confidence downgrades: claims sourced only from the researcher's search excerpts that could not be re-fetched in verification (web access blocked, search budget exhausted) were capped at moderate, including Sebeos's smoke-and-ladders passage, Howard-Johnston's reliability judgement, the communion scene, Hamazasp's curopalates title and al-Baladhuri's Dvin treaty text. Verification used an offline copy of the June 2023 English Wikipedia, Armenian Wikipedia extracts, and Lynch's Armenia (1901).

didYouKnow: replaced the mubarizun item (moderate, not re-verified) with the sourced Abeghian identification of Theodoros with K'eri T'oros of the David of Sasun epic, which strengthens the heroic framing without inventing anything.

Briefing rewritten to restore a heroic rally (230 words): adds Theodoros's rank as patrician, frames Zvartnots as a promise of endurance, and closes 'Dvin fell. At Artsap, Theodoros answered. Answer with him.', while keeping the truthful forward look at the pact and his death in Syria.

eras.era: Era 4: The Armenian highlands in the Ottoman-Safavid wars, 16th century AD (1514-1590); level set at Serdar Ferhad Pasha's advance from Kars on Erivan (Yerevan), August-September 1583
eras.dateRange: Battle of Chaldiran 23 August 1514. Ottoman-Safavid War of 1532-1555 (Van besieged and bombarded in 1548, passing to the Ottomans on 25 August 1548; Suleiman's campaign June 1554 to May 1555), ended by the Peace of Amasya, 29 May 1555. Ottoman-Safavid War of 1578-1590 (Lala Mustafa Pasha's campaign from spring 1578; Battle of Cildir 9 August 1578; Kars refortified, work completed 23 August 1579; Ferhad Pasha's army left Kars 11 August 1583 and entered Erivan without a fight about mid-September 1583, then built a fortress there in about 45 days; Ganja taken 1 September 1588), ended by the Treaty of Constantinople (Treaty of Ferhad Pasha), 21 March 1590. Ottoman rule at Erivan lasted until Shah Abbas I retook it in 1604, after a siege begun in November 1603. Date variant: English Wikipedia dates the Erivan fortress to 1582-1583; the detailed Turkish account places all of Ferhad's work there in autumn 1583.

briefing.title: The Crossing Between Empires
briefing.body:
For seventy years the Armenian highlands have been the road between two empires. In 1514 Sultan Selim's cannon and Janissaries broke Shah Ismail's horsemen at Chaldiran. In 1548 Suleiman's guns battered Van until it fell, and in 1555 the Peace of Amasya drew its line through Armenia itself: the west to the sultan, the east to the shah.

Now the war has come back. In 1578 Lala Mustafa Pasha led the sultan's army into the Caucasus, and the next year he raised the walls of Kars anew. In 1579 Ottoman raiders struck Erivan and carried off captives. This August the serdar Ferhad Pasha marched out of Kars. His goal is Erivan, and a fortress to hold it. The shah's governor is pulling back. If this plain is to be held, you will hold it.

No Armenian king rules here, and no royal army will meet him. In 1547 Catholicos Stepanos V gathered clergy and meliks in secret at Etchmiadzin, then carried their plea for Armenia's freedom to Venice and Rome. No help came, but the hope endured. In the mountains of Syunik and Karabakh the meliks still hold their lands.

This stand is not drawn from a single recorded battle. It honors the villagers, monks and melik retainers who lived in the path of these armies. Azabs, sipahis and musket-bearing Janissaries are on the road, and the siege guns roll behind them.

Ring the bell. Man the walls. Hold the line where history wavered, and show the column that this land is still defended.
briefing.stakes: A representative Armenian village and monastery on the Ararat plain, standing in the path of Ferhad Pasha's column as it marched from Kars to Erivan in August and September 1583.
briefing.victoryEpilogue: You held the line. In history, the shah's governor abandoned Erivan, Ferhad Pasha entered it without a fight in September 1583 and raised a new fortress there in about 45 days, and the 1590 treaty left the province to the Ottomans until Shah Abbas I retook Erivan in 1604. Armenia stayed divided between the empires, yet the Armenian meliks of Karabakh, whose semi-independent status Shah Abbas recognized in 1603, kept their hereditary domains until Russia abolished them in 1822.
briefing.defeatEpilogue: The column marched on, as the armies of both empires did for generations. Erivan changed hands again and again, and after retaking it in 1604 Shah Abbas I ordered the mass deportation of Armenians from the region deeper into Iran. Only the Treaty of Zuhab in 1639 brought a long pause, and the frontier it confirmed still split Armenia in two.
didYouKnow: The Peace of Amasya, signed on 29 May 1555, was the first treaty between the Ottomans and the Safavids, and it split Armenia between them, west and east.
At Chaldiran on 23 August 1514, Ottoman cannon and Janissary muskets fought behind a barrier of carts; the Safavid army had no artillery.
In 1547 Catholicos Stepanos V Salmastetsi called a secret council at Etchmiadzin, then took Armenia's appeal to Venice, to Popes Paul III and Julius III, and to Emperor Charles V.
Under the 1555 peace Kars was left neutral and its fortress was razed; Lala Mustafa Pasha rebuilt it for Sultan Murad III in 1579.
Ferhad Pasha's new fortress at Erivan went up in about 45 days in the autumn of 1583.
Ottoman deli horsemen wore feathered caps of leopard skin and decorated their shields with bird feathers.

keyFigures.name: Selim I
keyFigures.role: Ottoman sultan; victor at Chaldiran, 23 August 1514
keyFigures.note: His heavy artillery and Janissaries with firearms, behind a barrier of carts, defeated Shah Ismail's cavalry army; his troops took Tabriz on 7 September 1514, pillaged it and withdrew.

keyFigures.name: Shah Ismail I
keyFigures.role: Founder of the Safavid state; defeated at Chaldiran
keyFigures.note: Fought at Chaldiran without artillery, was wounded and nearly captured, and never again led a campaign; the Safavid state survived.

keyFigures.name: Suleiman I
keyFigures.role: Ottoman sultan; his army took Van (1548); campaigned June 1554 to May 1555; party to the Peace of Amasya (1555)
keyFigures.note: Van was besieged and bombarded in 1548 and passed to the Ottomans on 25 August 1548. Turkish Wikipedia says his 1554 army took Erivan, Karabakh and Nakhchivan, with Sokollu Mehmed Pasha as his deputy (moderate). The burning of part of Yerevan in 1554 rests on one weak page and is not used.

keyFigures.name: Shah Tahmasp I
keyFigures.role: Safavid shah; party to the Peace of Amasya, 29 May 1555
keyFigures.note: Avoided pitched battle in 1554 and struck Ottoman supply routes; the 1555 treaty left Eastern Armenia to Iran and Western Armenia to the Ottomans.

keyFigures.name: Murad III
keyFigures.role: Ottoman sultan who opened the war of 1578-1590
keyFigures.note: Kars was refortified in 1579 on his order, and Ganja was taken on 1 September 1588 on his order.

keyFigures.name: Lala Mustafa Pasha
keyFigures.role: Ottoman serdar (commander) of the 1578 Caucasian campaign
keyFigures.note: Under his command, a force led in the field by Dervish Pasha and decided by Ozdemiroglu Osman Pasha won at Cildir on 9 August 1578; Tiflis fell on 24 August. He refortified Kars, finishing on 23 August 1579, and was dismissed on 7 January 1580.

keyFigures.name: Koca Sinan Pasha
keyFigures.role: Ottoman commander on the eastern front from January 1580; later grand vizier
keyFigures.note: Replaced Lala Mustafa in 1580 and was Ferhad Pasha's bitter rival; he, not Ferhad, was Lala Mustafa's direct successor.

keyFigures.name: Serdar Ferhad Pasha
keyFigures.role: Ottoman serdar on the Iranian front from 1583 and again from 1586; recommended level boss
keyFigures.note: Of Albanian devshirme origin, former Agha of the Janissaries. Marched from Kars on 11 August 1583, fortified Suregel and Talin on the way, entered Erivan without a fight about mid-September after the Safavid governor withdrew, and built a fortress there in about 45 days. Took the Lori and Gori castles in 1584 and Ganja on 1 September 1588; the 1590 treaty bears his name. Grand vizier 1591-1592 and 1595. Not to be confused with Suleiman's son-in-law, also named Ferhad Pasha.

keyFigures.name: Mohammad Khan Tokhmaq Ustajlu
keyFigures.role: Safavid beglarbeg (governor) of Erivan, 1568-1575 and again from 1578
keyFigures.note: Commanded the Safavid-Georgian army defeated at Cildir in 1578. In 1583, with no reinforcements from Shah Mohammad Khodabanda, he evacuated Erivan rather than fight Ferhad's army (Turkish Wikipedia, moderate).

keyFigures.name: Shah Abbas I
keyFigures.role: Safavid shah from 1588
keyFigures.note: Accepted the 1590 peace, then retook Erivan in 1604 after a siege begun in November 1603. In 1603 he recognized the semi-independent status of the Karabakh meliks, and around 1604 he ordered the mass deportation of Armenians from his Armenian territories into Iran.

keyFigures.name: Stepanos V Salmastetsi
keyFigures.role: Catholicos of All Armenians, 1545-1567 (English Wikipedia's summary line gives 1547-1567)
keyFigures.note: In 1547 he convened a secret council of Eastern Armenian meliks and senior clergy at Etchmiadzin. He led its delegation to Venice (autumn 1548) and Rome (spring 1549), negotiated with Popes Paul III and Julius III, and in 1550 carried papal letters to Emperor Charles V and King Sigismund II Augustus of Poland. He returned in 1552 with no tangible result.

keyFigures.name: Mikayel I Sebastatsi
keyFigures.role: Coadjutor catholicos from 1547; Catholicos of All Armenians 1567-1576
keyFigures.note: Ran the see during Stepanos V's journey (1547-1552). In 1562 he convened a secret council at the Surb Nshan monastery in Sebastia, with both Western and Eastern Armenian leaders; on 20 May 1562 it sent petitions to Pope Pius IV through Abgar Dpir Tokhatetsi. No result followed (moderate).

keyFigures.name: Melik Hakhnazar I
keyFigures.role: Melik of Kashatagh, son of Melik Haykaz I; died 1551
keyFigures.note: In the early 16th century he moved the melikdom's seat from Kashatagh to Khnatsakh, where his mansion survives. His 1551 tombstone means he was dead long before 1583; do not depict him in this level.

keyFigures.name: Melik Haykaz II
keyFigures.role: Melik of Kashatagh, 1551-1623; son of Hakhnazar I
keyFigures.note: Pro-Iranian in the Ottoman-Safavid wars; per historian Morus Hasratyan he spent 10-15 years in exile in Iran during the Ottoman occupation of the 1580s-1590s and was restored around 1606-1607. Armenian Wikipedia's claims that he fought Ottoman-aligned forces and was held at Ganja are low confidence.

keyFigures.name: Alexander II of Kakheti
keyFigures.role: King of Kakheti, 1574-1605
keyFigures.note: Made peace with Lala Mustafa Pasha on 1 September 1578 and agreed to pay annual tribute. Turkish Wikipedia adds that he brought 5,000 men and supplied the Ottoman army on its march to the Shirvan border; he did not conquer Shirvan for the Ottomans.

keyFigures.name: Grigor Daranaghtsi (Kamakhetsi)
keyFigures.role: Armenian churchman and chronicler, c. 1576-1643
keyFigures.note: Wrote his Chronicle in 1634-1640 as an eyewitness to the events of his lifetime, with rich material on the Jalali revolts; useful for flavor text after 1590, not for 1583.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: Azabs were Ottoman irregular infantry. Under Suleiman's law codes one man was levied from every 20-30 households, and the others paid for his upkeep. Their main battle role was to fight as front-line archers ahead of the cannon and Janissaries, slow the enemy's first charge, and then draw aside so the guns and muskets could fire. Fortress azabs built bridges and worked as sappers.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Unarmored foot soldiers in long wool coats with red felt borks, the Janissary-style hat in a different color (attested). Mixed weapons, all attested for azabs: pole arms such as the harba spear and balta halberd, a few war scythes, maces, sabres and composite bows. Earthy coat colors (undyed wool, brown, madder) so they read as levies, not elites; the coat colors and any shields are unverified.
enemyRoster.justification: Azabs are attested as a 16th-century Ottoman corps, and their documented pole arms fit the spearmen slot well. No source consulted places azabs in Ferhad Pasha's 1583 column, so the label is plausible, not attested.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: Provincial cavalry who held timar land grants, served on campaign, kept order at home in peacetime, and formed the most numerous class in the classical Ottoman army. At Cildir in 1578 the force that first engaged the Safavids was provincial (eyalet) troops of the Diyarbakir governor, together with Kurdish beys.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: Horsemen in mail shirts with spired helmets and mail aventails, round shields, lances with small pennons, bow cases and sabres, in a fast silhouette with a raised lance. Gear details are standard iconography and were not verified.
enemyRoster.justification: Sipahis were the core of Ottoman field armies, and provincial troops fought on this front in 1578. The draft's claim that timariots were scattered at Chaldiran is not in the current Chaldiran article and was dropped. Akinji are a worse fit, since they were a Rumelian raiding force, decimated at Giurgiu in October 1595.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: The Sultan's standing infantry. By the early 16th century they were skilled with muskets, and at Chaldiran they fought with firearms behind a barrier of carts. In 1578 Lala Mustafa Pasha set out with the household (kapikulu) troops. They wore the bork hat and marched to the mehter.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: A tall white felt bork with a front holder for a spoon (attested), a long kaftan, a matchlock musket with smoking slow-match, a yatagan or kilij at the belt, and a disciplined, steady march. Colors were not verified.
enemyRoster.justification: The unit is attested on this front, at Chaldiran and with the 1578 household army. The heavy role is game license: Janissaries were not heavily armored, so their toughness stands for discipline. A short-range volley that briefly slows towers would show firepower rather than armor.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: Ottoman artillery decided Chaldiran (1514). Van was besieged and bombarded in 1548, with the French envoy Gabriel de Luetz advising on gun placement. In 1578 the vanguard under Behram Pasha advanced with cannon. In 1583 the Ottomans placed 50 sahi guns in the new Erivan fortress. Balyemez was the Ottoman name for a long-range bronze battery gun used above all to batter fortresses in the 16th and 17th centuries.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: A long bronze barrel on a heavy two-wheeled timber carriage, with a crew of 2 or 3 in plain kaftans carrying a rammer and a linstock, and wicker gabions set up when emplaced. A thick white smoke plume on firing. The bronze casting is attested for balyemez; the draft oxen and gabions are plausible but unverified.
enemyRoster.justification: Gunpowder artillery is the defining Ottoman advantage of the era and is attested on the Armenian plateau (Van 1548, the 1578 campaign, Erivan 1583). Erivan itself fell without a siege in 1583, so the guns in this level stand for the column's artillery train, not a recorded bombardment. The draft's 'kale-kob' term could not be re-verified and was replaced with balyemez, which was verified.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: Deli were Ottoman light cavalry known for reckless courage. In the 16th century they served under the beylerbeyi of Rumelia and the sanjak-beys of Smederevo and Bosnia, and only from the late 17th century under Anatolian viziers. They wore feathered caps of leopard or spotted-hyena skin, decorated their shields with bird feathers, and dressed in animal skins.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: A light horseman in a leopard-skin cloak and a feathered fur cap, with a feather-decked shield, lance and curved sabre. In game they ride the ridgelines and cliff ledges above the road, a separate elevated lane. Drop the single feathered wing: the claim that a deli wing inspired the Polish hussars could not be verified.
enemyRoster.justification: No flying units existed in 16th-century warfare, so the flyer becomes riders on high ground that only ranged towers (Highland Bowmen, Captured Tufenk Nest) can reach. Deli were a Balkan force in this century and are not documented on the 1583 Erivan front. If designers prefer a front-attested unit, Kurdish provincial levies fought with the Ottoman army at Cildir in 1578. 'Deli Hizir Pasha', the first Ottoman governor of Erivan, carried 'Deli' as a nickname and has nothing to do with this corps.

enemyRoster.historicalBasis: Ottoman commander-in-chief on the Iranian front from 1583. He marched from Kars on 11 August 1583, entered Erivan without a fight about mid-September, and built a fortress there in about 45 days. He took Ganja on 1 September 1588, where a fortress begun on 3 September was finished in about forty days, and gave his name to the treaty of 21 March 1590.
enemyRoster.visualNotes: A senior pasha on horseback in a large white turban and a fur-trimmed robe, escorted by mehter musicians with kettle drums (nakkare), big drums (kos), zurna shawms, trumpets and cymbals; these instruments are attested for the mehter. A horsetail standard behind him is unverified. Boss abilities: 'Mehter March' (+20% speed to enemies within 3 tiles for 6 s, every 20 s) and 'Fortress Builder' (raises an earthwork redoubt once per wave that gives emplaced Balyemez guns +1 tile of range).
enemyRoster.justification: Ferhad Pasha is the attested commander of the 1583 advance on Erivan. Defeating him in game is fiction, and the victory epilogue says that in history he took and fortified Erivan. Putting the mehter on the enemy side matches history, since it was the Janissaries' band.

towerAudit.reason: Bows were still front-line weapons in 16th-century warfare here: azabs fought as front-line archers ahead of the guns, and Janissaries began as archers. Local defenders with bows need no firearms they may not have had.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: Villagers and melik retainers on a stone parapet with composite bows, sheepskin hats, and wool coats in undyed and madder tones. Higher tiers add a mail shirt and helmet for retainers. Clothing details are unverified.

towerAudit.reason: No evidence was found for torsion ballistae in 16th-century Armenia; the era's long-range weapons were muskets and cannon. Whether Armenian villagers owned firearms is unverified, so the reskin presents the guns as captured Ottoman weapons (game license).
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: Two defenders behind a stone breastwork with long matchlock muskets taken from Janissaries, a coil of smoking slow-match and a forked rest, and a white puff of smoke on each shot. It keeps the slot's single-target, high-damage, long-range role and can hit Deli Ridge-Riders.

towerAudit.reason: By this era gunpowder artillery had replaced mechanical engines as the big siege weapons, and Armenian villagers owning cannon is unverified and unlikely. Dropping stones from the heights needs no special technology and keeps the area-damage role. This is game license; no specific 16th-century episode was found.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: A timber cradle braced on the hillside above the road, stacked with boulders. Defenders knock out a wedge and the stones bounce down a scree chute in a dust cloud, doing area damage where they land. It cannot hit ridge-riding Deli.

towerAudit.reason: A Zoroastrian fire altar belongs to the Sasanian enemy of the 451 level and has no place among 16th-century Christian Armenian defenders under a Catholicos at Etchmiadzin. Pouring burning pitch from walls is a generic fortification practice; no 16th-century Armenian instance was verified.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: An iron cauldron on a wall-top hearth with black smoke. Defenders tip burning pitch and throw clay fire-pots onto the road, leaving a burning pool that does damage over time.

towerAudit.reason: A rallying support aura works, but in this era the war drums belong to the Ottoman mehter, the enemy's band. A monastery bell suits the defenders: Armenian monasteries had bell towers long before 1583, at Sanahin (first quarter of the 13th century) and Haghpat (free-standing belfry of 1245). Using the bell as a call to arms is game license.
towerAudit.eraReskinVisual: A small stone belfry on columns with a bronze bell rung by a monk in a black hooded habit, with sound-ring pulses spreading over nearby towers. Same buff numbers as War Drums; the drums move to the enemy boss as the mehter.

mechanicAudit.existingMechanic: Ottoman bombards (cannon) that counter-fire on towers
mechanicAudit.reason: Ottoman guns battering defenses is well attested: artillery decided Chaldiran in 1514, Van was bombarded in 1548, the 1578 vanguard marched with cannon, 50 sahi guns were placed in the Erivan fortress in 1583, and Shah Abbas put cannon on siege towers against Erivan in 1604. Big guns were slow, had to be emplaced, and hit fortifications rather than sniping single defenders. 'Bombard' is a European term (in use from the 14th century) and not the Ottoman name; balyemez is the period Ottoman term for a fortress-battering battery gun. Keep the mechanic, but make it slow and telegraphed, and have it disable towers rather than destroy them.
mechanicAudit.proposal: Balyemez Battery Gun: moves at 0.5x spearman speed and can fire only from 3 marked battery spots. Emplacing takes 4 s (gabions appear), during which it takes +50% damage. Once emplaced it fires every 8 s at the tower with the highest total upgrade cost within 6 tiles, after a 1.5 s telegraph (red arc plus smoking linstock). A hit 'breaches' the tower: disabled for 5 s (3 s at tier 3 and above, and 1 s less if a Monastery Bell covers it). No permanent destruction. Each gun has 2 crew sprites; killing both (Rain of Arrows is ideal) silences it for 10 s until a replacement crew walks up from the rear. Frost pauses its reload timer for the spell's duration. At most 2 guns on the map at once, first appearing in wave 4. Boss link: Ferhad Pasha's 'Fortress Builder' redoubt gives guns emplaced next to it +1 tile of range, a nod to his fortress building at Erivan (about 45 days, 1583) and Ganja (about 40 days, 1588).

eras.heroNote: Vardan Mamikonian is not appropriate as a living hero in 1583. He died at Avarayr in 451 (English Wikipedia gives 2 June 451; the game's Era 2 dateline uses 26 May, a variant not verified here), more than eleven centuries earlier. Continuity is still possible and true to the period: he is venerated as a saint of the Armenian Apostolic Church, with a feast on the last Thursday before Great Lent, so a 'Banner of Saint Vardan' relic or hero skin carried by 16th-century defenders is defensible game license. Recommended period-correct swap: 'the Melik', an archetype hereditary Armenian lord. English Wikipedia counts 70-90 melik houses in Eastern Armenia, including in the Yerevan, Lori, Syunik and Karabakh areas. If a named hero is wanted, the best-attested contemporary is Melik Haykaz II of Kashatagh (ruled 1551-1623), son of Melik Hakhnazar I. Per English Wikipedia, citing Morus Hasratyan, he backed Iran in the Ottoman-Safavid wars and spent 10-15 years in exile in Iran during the Ottoman occupation of the 1580s-1590s. Armenian Wikipedia's accounts that he fought Ottoman-aligned forces, was held captive at Ganja, and was called 'Goja Aslan' (old lion) by Shah Abbas I are low confidence, the nickname resting on tradition. No source places him on the Ararat plain in 1583, so use him only as a contemporary rallying figure, never as the victor of a recorded battle. Melik Hakhnazar I died in 1551 and cannot appear. Documented Armenian armed resistance to Ottoman armies in Syunik and Karabakh (Davit Bek, died 1728) belongs to the 1720s.

mapRecommendation.reason: The level's attested target is Erivan on the Ararat plain: by 1583 the Ottomans held the Erivan province, and the 1590 treaty ceded it to them. A river-plain map with farmland fits a column descending on Erivan, and the season is now supported: Ferhad Pasha's army left Kars on 11 August 1583 and entered Erivan about mid-September, so a late-summer harvest palette is accurate (moderate confidence). The column did not need to cross the Araxes itself: its attested route ran from Kars through Suregel (the Shirak plateau west of Gyumri) and Talin, and Erivan stands on the Zangi (Hrazdan), an Araxes tributary. The 'crossing' is therefore game license; labeling the in-level river the Zangi would be more exact. Gyumri Road follows the real approach through Shirak, but its winter snow contradicts the August-September march; it would fit only if the snow were removed. Lori Gates is a fair third choice, since Ferhad Pasha took Lori castle in 1584.
mapRecommendation.mapAnachronisms: Tushpa Vale: Tushpa was the Urartian capital later known as Van. In this era the city is Van, bombarded and taken by the Ottomans in 1548, so label it 'Van' or 'Van Shore' for Era 4. Gyumri Road: 'Gyumri' is the modern name. The place was anciently Kumayri, worn down to Kumri and Gumri; the Turkish form is Gumru. The surrounding plateau appears in Ottoman usage as Suregel (Shoragyal). Kumayri belonged to the Safavid Erivan province from 1502. 'Alexandropol' dates from 1837 and must not appear. Araxes Crossing: 'Araxes' is the classical Greek name; the historical Armenian name is Yeraskh and the Turkish and Persian form is Aras. Label the city Erivan or, in Ottoman and Persian usage, Revan. Do not show the Ottoman fortress as standing before autumn 1583. Armenian tradition says Ferhad Pasha used stones from ruined churches and graves in it (low confidence), so if the fortress appears, avoid showing churches intact inside its walls. Lori Gates: Lori fortress passed between Turks, Persians and sometimes Georgians from 1562 to 1734, and Ferhad took it in 1584. Sanahin and Haghpat monasteries are 10th-century foundations with 13th-century belfries, so medieval stone churches with bell towers are accurate scenery for 1583. The draft's 'do not place meliks in Lori' is wrong: English Wikipedia lists Lori among the provinces with melik houses.

corrections: Stepanos V's reign: draft said 1547-1567; correct is 1545-1567 per Armenian Wikipedia 'Stepanos E Salmastetsi' (English Wikipedia's summary line says 1547, but its own text says he was elected in 1545). Marked moderate.

Stepanos V's mission: draft said he went 'to the Pope'. Corrected per Armenian Wikipedia: Venice (autumn 1548), Rome (spring 1549) with Popes Paul III and Julius III, then papal letters to Charles V and Sigismund II Augustus (1550), return in 1552 with no tangible result. The briefing now says 'Venice and Rome' and 'No help came'.

Erivan in 1583: draft said Ferhad Pasha 'besieged Yerevan'. Correct per Turkish Wikipedia 'Revan'in Zapti' and English Wikipedia 'Mohammad Khan Tokhmaq Ustajlu': the Safavid governor Tokhmaq Khan evacuated, and the Ottomans entered without fighting about mid-September 1583. Siege wording removed; the victory epilogue now says he entered 'without a fight'.

Erivan fortress date: draft said 1582-1583. Ferhad was not appointed serdar until 1583, and the detailed Turkish account puts the 45-day construction in autumn 1583. Now given as 1583, with English Wikipedia's 1582-1583 noted as a variant.

Command succession: draft called Ferhad 'commander-in-chief after Lala Mustafa'. Correct per Turkish Wikipedia '1578-1590 Osmanli-Safevi Savasi': Lala Mustafa was dismissed on 7 January 1580 and replaced by Koca Sinan Pasha, and Ferhad became serdar in 1583. Koca Sinan added to keyFigures.

Cildir: draft credited Lala Mustafa personally. Per English and Turkish Wikipedia, the battle was fought by his subordinates (Dervish Pasha, decided by Ozdemiroglu Osman Pasha) against Tokhmaq Khan. Wording adjusted; the 9 August 1578 date is confirmed.

Van 1548: draft said guns 'bombarded Van on 25 August 1548'. Per Turkish Wikipedia, 25 August 1548 is when the siege ended and Van passed to the Ottomans, with Ulama Pasha completing it; English Wikipedia confirms the bombardment but gives no day.

Yerevan 1554: draft's briefing said Ottomans 'seized Yerevan and set part of it ablaze', sourced to a travel site. The burning appears only on English Wikipedia 'History of Yerevan', which has clear errors; Turkish Wikipedia supports only that the 1554 army took Erivan, Karabakh and Nakhchivan. Removed from the briefing; the burning claim is kept at low confidence.

Treaty of Zuhab: draft's defeat epilogue said the struggle 'ended only with the Treaty of Zuhab in 1639'. Per English Wikipedia 'Treaty of Zuhab', border disputes continued, and per Lynch (1901) and Eversley (1917) the Ottomans took Erivan again in 1724. Reworded to 'brought a long pause'.

Kars: draft said only that Kars was 'wrecked by Timur'. Per English Wikipedia 'Peace of Amasya', under the 1555 treaty Kars was declared neutral and its fortress destroyed, which was the state Lala Mustafa found. The didYouKnow is rewritten, and completion of the Kars works (23 August 1579, 27 days) is added per Turkish Wikipedia.

Alexander II of Kakheti: draft said he 'helped Lala Mustafa Pasha conquer Shirvan'. Per English Wikipedia he made peace on 1 September 1578 and paid tribute; Turkish Wikipedia adds only that he supplied the army as far as the Shirvan border.

Ganja 1588: draft said 'Ferhad Pasha defeated the Qajars near the Aras'. Per Turkish Wikipedia, the 29 September 1588 Aras battle was won by a corps under Cafer Pasha against Ziyadoglu Mehmed Khan, and the Safavids had evacuated Ganja without a fight.

Turkish Wikipedia gives feathered caps of leopard or spotted-hyena skin, feather-decked shields and bear-skin trousers. The wing-to-hussar link is unverified (English Wikipedia 'Polish hussars' gives no such origin), so the wing was dropped from the visuals. Also noted: 'Deli Hizir Pasha' is a nickname, not the unit.

Season: draft marked the harvest setting unverified. Turkish Wikipedia gives departure from Kars on 11 August and entry into Erivan in mid-September 1583, so a late-summer setting is supported (moderate). The dateline is now 'September 1583'.

Route and map: draft did not give the column's route. Per Turkish Wikipedia it went from Kars via Suregel (the Shirak plateau west of Gyumri) and Talin, so Gyumri Road is the geographic approach (but not in snow), and Araxes Crossing is kept for its season and plain with the 'crossing' flagged as game license.
Monastery bells: draft marked them unverified. English Wikipedia dates the bell towers at Sanahin to the early 13th century and at Haghpat to 1245. Upgraded to moderate.

Vardan: draft left the date and commemoration unverified. English Wikipedia gives Avarayr as 2 June 451 (the 26 May variant used elsewhere in the game is not verified here) and confirms his sainthood and feast on the last Thursday before Great Lent.

Lori 1562-1734: draft sourced this to a search summary. Now confirmed in Armenian Wikipedia 'Lori berd' (the English article omits it), and Ferhad's capture of Lori in 1584 was added per Turkish Wikipedia.
Gumru and Aras/Yeraskh: draft marked these low or unverified. Gumru is now confirmed by Turkish Wikipedia and Aras/Yeraskh by English Wikipedia 'Aras (river)'.

Briefing length and tone: the rewrite keeps the heroic rally, adds true dramatic beats (the 1579 raid, the shah's governor pulling back, 'No help came, but the hope endured') and drops the unverifiable 1554 burning. It is 254 words.

Peace of Amasya 'first division of historical Armenia': this is true only as the first Ottoman-Safavid division, since Armenia had been partitioned between Rome and Persia in 387. The didYouKnow is reworded as the first Ottoman-Safavid treaty splitting Armenia.
Grigor Daranaghtsi: dates kept (c. 1576-1643), and his Chronicle (1634-1640) is flagged as useful only for after 1590, not for 1583.
Cildir 'about 150 km southwest of Tiflis' and Malkhasyan demography claims from the draft were not re-verified and were removed as unneeded.

mapAssignment.reason: Tushpa, the Urartian capital on the Rock of Van by the eastern shore of Lake Van, is where Tiglath-pileser III's annals place the 735 BC confrontation: Sarduri II shut in the city, battle before the gates, citadel not taken (high for what the annals say; the source is the Assyrian king's own account). 'Tushpa' is the Urartian name, so the label is already period-correct (Assyrian form Turushpa; later Tosp/Van). Art fixes: remove the medieval and Ottoman structures of Van Fortress and show Urartian large-block masonry. The lake carries the outflanker water lane. Uncontested: the Arab dossier's Lake Van alternative (Rshtunik, Aghtamar) is on the south shore, not at Tushpa.

mapAssignment.era: Era 2: Sasanian Persia vs the Armenian nakharars, Avarayr, 451 AD
mapAssignment.reason: The battle was fought on the Avarayr plain along the Tghmut (today's Zangmar), an Araxes tributary, near Churs and Maku in Artaz (moderate-high: Wikipedia 'Avarayr Plain', 'Zangmar River', Hewsen in Iranica per dossier). It is the only river-plain map, and the game already pairs it with this level. 'Araxes Crossing' is wrong for 451 because the fighting was on the Tghmut, not the Araxes. Palette: the battle fell in late May or early June 451, so a ripe golden harvest is doubtful (local harvest timing unverified); re-tint toward early-summer green or tag the palette as license. No monasteries or khachkars (first true khachkars 9th c.). The Arab and Ottoman dossiers also asked for this map; both were moved because Avarayr has no other fitting map, while they do.

The 643 invasion ravaged Ayrarat and was defeated by Theodoros Rshtuni (high: Wikipedia 'Arminiya', 'Muslim conquest of Armenia'). Both Shirak (the Gyumri district) and Kogovit (canton of the fortress of Artsap) were cantons of Ayrarat (moderate: English Wikipedia 'Gyumri'; Armenian Wikipedia 'Vaspurakan' calls it 'Ayrarat's Kogovit'), so 'Ayrarat Road' is true whichever canton the art evokes. 'Gyumri' is modern (Leninakan 1924-1990, Kumayri 1990-1992, Gyumri from 1992, per Wikipedia 'Gyumri'), and 'Kumayri' itself is attested only from Ghevond the Historian (8th c.); the claimed Urartian 'Kumayri' is unverified in all four dossiers. Snow: the season of the 643 raid is unverified, so snow is tagged game license; the Arab dossier's optional Highland Cold rule was designed for this winter map and its tooltip must cite Vardanakert, winter 703. Remove any 19th-century or later buildings. Alternative label if the Artsap relief stays central: 'Kogovit Road'.

mapAssignment.era: Era 4: Ottoman-Safavid wars, 16th c. AD (re-anchored to Lori, 1584)
mapAssignment.reason: This is the only era in which the map's monasteries are correct: Sanahin (10th c.; bell tower first quarter of the 13th c.) and Haghpat (probably 976; free-standing belfry 1245) stood in 1584 (moderate-high: Wikipedia 'Sanahin Monastery', 'Haghpat Monastery'), and the Era 4 'Monastery Bell' support tower now matches real belfries on the map. Lori Fortress is 11th century (capital of the Tashir-Dzoraget kingdom from 1065), so 'Lori' is period-correct. Turkish Wikipedia 'Serdar Ferhat Pasa' says that in 1584 Ferhad Pasha, giving military support to Tiflis, took the castles of Lori and Gori (moderate, single source); Armenian Wikipedia 'Lori berd' says Lori passed between Ottomans, Safavids and sometimes Georgians from 1562 to 1734 (moderate). Consequence: the Ottoman level moves from 'Erivan, September 1583' to 'Lori, 1584', with Ferhad's bloodless entry into Erivan (mid-September 1583) kept as backstory. Gyumri Road, which follows Ferhad's real 1583 route through Suregel, was rejected because its snow contradicts an August-September march.

towerReskinTable.note: Direct fire; can target outflankers (flyers). Bows are attested in every era: inscribed royal quivers from Teishebaini (Karmir Blur); Persian archery in Ammianus 25.1.13; smoke and arrows clearing Dvin's walls in 640 (history attributed to Sebeos); azabs fighting as front-line archers ahead of the Ottoman guns. Eras 2 and 3 share the name on purpose: both armies were raised by noble houses, each nakharar with his own troops (Wikipedia 'Nakharar', 'Sparapet' quoting Adontz). Vary kit, not name (451: mail or quilted coats; 643: conical iron helmets). No invented heraldry in any era.

Single target, long range, direct fire; can target outflankers. Era 1: no mechanical artillery before 399 BC (Diodorus via Marsden), so hand-hurled spears. Era 2: ballista described by Ammianus 23.4.1-3; none recorded at Avarayr (license); never call it 'scorpio' (in Ammianus's day that meant the onager). Era 3: weakest-attested slot, since traction machines had largely displaced torsion engines by the late 6th c.; drop 'Byzantine' from the draft name because no source places such an engine on an Armenian wall in 640-655 (license). Era 4: matchlocks presented as captured because Armenian villagers' firearms are unverified; 'Musket' replaces the draft 'Tufenk', which clashed with the dossier's 'tufekci' spelling.

Area damage, lobbed; cannot target outflankers. Era 1: defenders throwing stones from turrets is shown on Assyrian siege reliefs. Era 2: one-armed torsion onager per Ammianus 23.4.4-7. Era 3: pull-crew traction trebuchet (Avaro-Slav use at Thessalonica 586; Arab adoption second half of the 7th c.). No artillery is recorded at Avarayr or in Armenia 640-655 specifically, so Eras 2 and 3 are license. Never show a counterweight trebuchet (12th c.) in any era, and no traction trebuchet before Era 3. Era 4: gunpowder had replaced mechanical engines, so a hillside rock chute (license).

Burn damage over time; cannot target outflankers. No era shows a fire altar on the defenders' side: no Urartian fire cult was found; in 451 the fire altar is the persecutor's symbol (a fire temple was installed in Etchmiadzin Cathedral in 450, and Nvarsak's first reported term removed fire-altars); the defenders of 643 and 1584 were Christian. Era 2 is renamed from the dossier's 'Martyrs' Chapel' so the church is not the weapon and clergy stay in the support slot; its fire attack rests on Ammianus 19.7.7 (firebrands drove Persian elephants back at Amida, 359). Era 3 rests on the Petra fire-pots (550-551, Procopius); never label it Greek fire, which is first used in the 670s. Rename the base slot in the UI to a neutral 'Fire Tower'.

Support aura with identical numbers in every era. Drums are unverified for the defenders in all four eras, and in Era 4 they belong to the enemy's mehter, so no defender tower uses drums; rename the base slot in the UI to a neutral 'Rally Tower'. Era 1 rests on the annal formula 'Haldi went forth with his weapon' and dedicated temple weapons. Era 2 label and codex must say 'Ghevond the Priest' (Leontius of Vanand) to avoid confusion with Ghevond the Historian (8th c.) cited in Era 3. Era 3 horns and cross finial are license. Era 4 bell matches the real 13th-century belfries at Sanahin and Haghpat on the Lori map; its use as a call to arms is license.

heroPerEra.title: Sarduri, son of Argishti, King of Biainili
heroPerEra.justification: The king Tiglath-pileser III's annals say was shut up in Turushpa in 735 BC while the citadel held (high for the annal statement; it is the enemy king's own account). Son of Argishti I (high). Bronze helmets and a quiver from Teishebaini (Karmir Blur) bear his name (moderate), which gives a sourced visual kit. Reign dates differ between sources (c. 755-735 BC in Britannica, 764-735 BC in Wikipedia, other estimates), so game text gives no regnal years. Do not give him the title 'lord of the city of Tushpa', which is documented here only on a shield of his son Rusa. Vardan does not appear: he lived about 1,185 years later.

heroPerEra.title: Vardan Mamikonian, Sparapet of Armenia
heroPerEra.justification: Hereditary sparapet of the Mamikonian house and leader of the 450-451 revolt, killed at Avarayr in 451 with eight of his commanders (high). Venerated as a saint; Vardanants falls on the last Thursday before Great Lent (high). This is the only era where the game's existing hero belongs. Because he died in the battle, his fall and revive are framed as martyrdom (Vardanants), never as survival. His nephew Vahan Mamikonian (Treaty of Nvarsak, 484) may appear in the epilogue or as an unlock.

heroPerEra.title: Theodoros Rshtuni, Lord of Rshtunik, Commander of the Armenian Forces
heroPerEra.justification: Defeated the Arab invasion of Ayrarat in 643 and was then recognized as ruler of Armenia by Constans II (high for the victory, moderate for the recognition date). Made commander-in-chief and patrikios by Constans II in 641 on Catholicos Nerses III's advice (moderate). Rshtunik lay on the south shore of Lake Van, with Aghtamar as his seat and refuge (moderate). His 652 or 653 pact with Muawiya is presented as strategic survival, neither betrayal nor triumph. 'Sparapet' is kept out of his in-game title so that Era 2's hereditary Mamikonian office stays clear; the codex can note that Wikipedia also calls him sparapet.

heroPerEra.title: Melik of the Highlands, hereditary Armenian lord
heroPerEra.justification: No well-attested Armenian commander fought Ferhad Pasha's columns in 1583-1584 (negative result across the Era 4 sources, moderate). English Wikipedia counts 70-90 melik houses in Eastern Armenia, Lori among their provinces (moderate), so an unnamed melik is true to the period and puts no real person where he was not. Rejected: Melik Haykaz II of Kashatagh (per Morus Hasratyan, in exile in Iran during the Ottoman occupation of the 1580s-1590s, and not near Lori); Melik Hakhnazar I (died 1551); Davit Bek (1720s). Optional cosmetic: a 'Banner of Saint Vardan' carried by the melik's retainers, since Vardan's veneration is attested.

harmony.flyerPolicy: One rule for all four eras: the flyer archetype is an outflanking unit, never a flying creature. No era had aerial combatants, so each flyer is a human troop type attested for that era's army, moving on a second lane (water or high ground) that bypasses the road. The anti-air rule is identical everywhere: only the direct-fire slots (the Archers slot and the Ballista slot) can target outflankers; the Catapult slot (lobbed), the Fire slot (ground burn) and the support slot cannot. Every flyer codex entry carries a 'Game license' tag saying what is attested and what is not. Era 1: Skin-Float Raiders on a Lake Van water lane (skin-float crossing attested on Ashurnasirpal II's 9th-century relief; use at Tushpa not recorded). Era 2: replace the Royal Hunting Falcon, the only animal flyer and an invented combat use, with a 'Tghmut Fording Party' of Sasanian light infantry wading a river lane on the Plain of Avarayr (Sasanian infantry attested; a fording move at Avarayr not recorded). Era 3: Ridge Climbers on a high lane above Ayrarat Road (no specific episode located). Era 4: Deli Ridge-Riders on the Lori gorge ledges (deli attested in the 16th-century Ottoman army, but as a Balkan force; if a front-attested unit is preferred, use Kurdish provincial horsemen, who fought with the Ottomans at Cildir in 1578). No wings on any unit: drop the deli wing. Show elevation with drop shadows and water lanes with wakes.
harmony.spellNotes: Keep all three names in every era. They name effects, not historical events, and identical names keep the UI stable while gameplay stays identical. Rain of Arrows fits all four eras because archery is attested in each (royal Urartian quivers from Teishebaini; Persian archery in Ammianus; smoke and arrows at Dvin in 640 per the history attributed to Sebeos; azab archers ahead of the Ottoman guns), and it is the natural counter to the Era 4 gun crews. Frost is plain weather and suits a highland campaign; it already hooks into era mechanics (disperses Era 3 smoke clouds, lasts 50% longer in Ayrarat Road cold snaps, pauses Era 4 balyemez reloads). Its Era 3 flavor must not claim a 7th-century cold-weather defeat: the attested frozen-river episode is Vardanakert, winter 703, recorded by Ghevond the Historian. Lightning needs one rule: no tooltip may present it as a recorded miracle or divine intervention, especially in the Christian eras, since no source records one at Tushpa, Avarayr, Artsap or Lori. Per-era flavor goes in a subtitle, never a rename. The one well-grounded option is Era 1 Lightning subtitled 'Teisheba's Storm': Teisheba was the Urartian god of thunder and storms, in the ruling triad with Haldi and Shivini (moderate, Wikipedia 'Urartu'), and the fortress Teishebaini was named for him. Eras 2 to 4 use a neutral subtitle such as 'Highland storm'.
harmony.campaignIntro:
For more than two thousand years, the armies of empires have marched into the Armenian highlands, the country of Lake Van, Mount Ararat and the Araxes. Now you command its defenders.

Your road begins in Biainili, the kingdom the Assyrians called Urartu, forerunner kingdom of the Armenian highlands. It is 735 BC. Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria has come to the foot of Tushpa, where King Sarduri II stands shut behind the walls on the rock. From there the road runs to the plain of Avarayr in 451, where Vardan Mamikonian and the Armenian princes took up arms to keep their Christian faith; to Ayrarat in 643, where Theodoros Rshtuni rode out against an Arab army; and to the gorge of Lori in 1584, as Ottoman and Safavid armies fought over a divided land.

Not every stand held. Each briefing tells you what truly happened. Where history held, hold with it. Where history wavered, hold the line.
harmony.campaignOutro: Four stands across more than two thousand years. The rock of Tushpa held, and Yerevan still traces its founding to Erebuni, raised in 782 BC by Argishti I, father of Sarduri II. Vardan fell at Avarayr, yet the struggle outlived him: in 484 the Treaty of Nvarsak granted Armenia freedom of worship, and the Armenian Church still honors him and his companions on Vardanants. Theodoros Rshtuni won his fight in Ayrarat, then bargained for terms that let Armenia keep its own cavalry and kept Arab garrisons out of its fortresses. Through the Ottoman-Safavid wars, villagers, monks and meliks endured as the borders moved over them. History did not always hold the line. You did, and now you know where it held and where it broke.
crossEraIssues: Map conflict: the Avarayr, Arab and Ottoman dossiers all chose Araxes Crossing. Resolved one-to-one: Avarayr keeps it (no other river plain fits), Arab moves to Gyumri Road renamed 'Ayrarat Road', Ottoman moves to Lori Gates. Each moved dossier must update its mapRecommendation, and Era 3 must add a 'game license' tag for the snow.

Era 4 re-anchoring required by the Lori assignment: dateline 'Ararat plain, Erivan, September 1583' becomes 'Lori, 1584'; the briefing's 'This August the serdar Ferhad Pasha marched out of Kars. His goal is Erivan' becomes backstory (he entered Erivan without a fight in mid-September 1583 and built a fortress there in about 45 days) followed by the 1584 turn north, when, giving military support to Tiflis, he took the castles of Lori and Gori (Turkish Wikipedia, moderate). Stakes and both epilogues must describe Lori, not Erivan; the victory epilogue can add that Lori changed hands between Ottomans, Safavids and sometimes Georgians from 1562 to 1734 (Armenian Wikipedia, moderate). Bonus: 'For seventy years' (1514 to 1583 is 69) becomes exact for 1584.

Avarayr day: Era 2 reports both 26 May and 2 June 451; Era 3's heroNote says '2 June 451 per Wikipedia'; Era 4's heroNote says the Era 2 dateline uses 26 May, which is stale (the dateline is now 'spring 451'). The offline June 2023 English Wikipedia is itself inconsistent ('Battle of Avarayr', 'Vardan Mamikonian', 'Yazdegerd II': 2 June; 'Churs': 26 May; 'Vahan I Mamikonian': both). Fix: all game text says '451' or 'spring 451'; only the codex mentions both days.

Two different men named Ghevond: Era 2's priest who addressed the army before Avarayr (Leontius of Vanand, St. Ghevond the Priest, executed 455) and Era 3's 8th-century historian whose account of Vardanakert (703) drives the Highland Cold tooltip. Fix: always write 'Ghevond the Priest' in Era 2 and 'Ghevond the Historian' in Era 3.

Sparapet: Era 2 calls it the hereditary Mamikonian office; Era 3's heroNote calls Theodoros Rshtuni 'sparapet'. Both are supported (Wikipedia 'Theodore Rshtuni' uses the word), but players will read a contradiction. Fix: Era 2 says 'hereditary sparapet of the Mamikonian house'; Era 3 in-game text says 'commander of the Armenian forces', as its briefing already does.

Fire slot: Era 2's 'Martyrs' Chapel' throws fire while Era 2's support slot is also clergy, and every other era treats the fire slot as a defenders' incendiary weapon. Fix: rename to 'Firebrand Rampart' (Ammianus 19.7.7) and change the Era 2 Panic mechanic text from 'Martyrs' Chapel fire hit' to 'Firebrand Rampart hit'. The base UI names 'Fire Altar' and 'War Drums' are wrong in all four eras; rename the base slots to neutral 'Fire Tower' and 'Rally Tower'.
Flyer: Era 2's Royal Hunting Falcon is the only animal flyer and its combat use is invented. Fix: replace with a 'Tghmut Fording Party' under the single flyer policy.

Bosses: Era 2's boss withdraws at 0 HP because Mushkan survived; the others die. Fix: one rule, historical commanders who survived withdraw at 0 HP (Tiglath-pileser III withdrew from Tushpa; Mushkan survived wounded; Ferhad Pasha lived to be grand vizier in 1591-1592 and 1595).

Era 3 boss: Habib ibn Maslama is out of date for a 643 level in both chronologies (Muslim sources put his Armenian campaign in 645/646, Armenian and Byzantine sources in 653/654-655). Fix: the boss becomes an unnamed 'Commander of the Ayrarat Raid' (Armenian Wikipedia says the force at Artsap had two commanders and names neither); keep Habib for the epilogue and codex.

Spelling harmonization for all game text: Tiglath-pileser (not Tiglath-Pileser); Vardan Mamikonian (codex may add Mamikonean); Yeghishe (not Elishe); Ghazar Parpetsi; Theodoros Rshtuni (not Theodore); Muawiya (Era 3 currently mixes 'Muawiya' and 'Mu'awiya'); Tushpa (Assyrian Turushpa only in quotes from the annals); Erivan for 1583-1584, Yerevan only for present-day statements; 'Captured Musket Nest' instead of 'Tufenk', which clashed with 'tufekci'.

River naming: Era 1 says the Urartian name of the river is unverified, Era 3 gives Yeraskh/Arax, Era 4 Yeraskh/Aras. Fix: the narrator uses 'Araxes' as the conventional English name in every era; period forms go only in the codex.

Lori Fortress date: Era 2 says it 'dates to 1065', Era 3 says '11th century, capital from 1065'. Wikipedia 'Lori Fortress': an 11th-century fortress built by David Anhoghin to become the capital of the Tashir-Dzoraget kingdom in 1065. Fix: use that wording everywhere.

Monastery dates are repeated in four dossiers with slightly different wording (Era 1 'Haghpat built 10th to 13th c.'). Fix: one codex line: Sanahin founded in the 10th c. (first church 930s-940s), bell tower first quarter of the 13th c.; Haghpat founded probably in 976, belfry 1245.

Gyumri renaming: Era 1 gives Leninakan 1924 to 1990, Era 3 says the name Gyumri was chosen in 1992. Both are right: Kumayri was used from 1990 to 1992 (Wikipedia 'Gyumri'). Moot in game text now that the map is 'Ayrarat Road'. All dossiers agree the Urartian 'Kumayri' claim is unverified; keep it out.

743 BC battle site: Era 1 says Kummuh (Radner; Wikipedia 'Sarduri II'), but Wikipedia 'Tiglath-Pileser III' says 'near Arpad' and has Sarduri pursued 'all the way back to Tushpa' in 743, which conflates 743 with 735. Keep Era 1 as written: Kummuh in 743, Turushpa in 735 (Eponym Chronicle).
Sarduri II reign dates vary (c. 755-735 Britannica; 764-735 Wikipedia; c. 763-735 and c. 756-730 elsewhere). Fix: no regnal years in game text.
Era 1 victory epilogue states 'no Assyrian army reached the Urartian capital again' as fact, but it rests on one source (Radner). Fix: 'no later Assyrian army is known to have reached Tushpa'.

Motto duplication: 'Hold the line where history wavered' closes both the Era 2 and Era 4 briefings and now also the campaign intro. Fix: keep it in the intro and in Era 2, where history did waver at Avarayr; end Era 4 on 'Ring the bell. Man the walls.' Era 1's 'Commander, the beacons are lit' stays unique to Era 1.
Avarayr palette: 'golden harvest' conflicts with a late May or early June battle. Fix: re-tint toward early-summer green or tag the palette as license.

Era 3 Zvartnots: the briefing says Nerses III 'is raising' Zvartnots in 643, while the didYouKnow says 'begun in the 640s' and the 643 start rests on an unrefetched excerpt. Fix: 'in these years Catholicos Nerses III is raising Zvartnots' and '640s' everywhere.

Era 3 route of the 643 invasion: English Wikipedia contradicts itself ('from the direction of Azerbaijan ... reached the Anatolian peninsula' in 'Muslim conquest of Armenia' versus 'from the direction of Arran ... reached Iberia' in 'Arminiya'). Fix: give no direction of approach in game text.

Duplicated codex facts: the traction trebuchet chronology (Thessalonica 586, Persian and Arab adoption) appears in both Era 2 and Era 3, and the Vardan death notice appears in Eras 1, 3 and 4. Fix: one shared codex entry for each, linked from every era.

Hero continuity: Vardan, the game's only hero, appears in Era 2 only. Eras 1, 3 and 4 use Sarduri II, Theodoros Rshtuni and the unnamed Melik, with an identical kit and per-era skins. Era 4 must not use Melik Haykaz II as a field hero, since he is recorded as in exile in Iran during the Ottoman occupation.
remainingUnverified: Verification limits of this pass: the WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200 of 200) and iranicaonline.org and en.wikipedia.org were blocked by the egress proxy. Spot-checks used the offline June 2023 Wikipedia texts (English, Turkish, Armenian) cached in this session's scratchpad. Scholarly works (Iranica, Cambridge History of Iran, Hewsen, Radner, Thomson's Sebeos) were not opened directly.
Exact day of Avarayr: 26 May or 2 June 451; sources disagree.
Ferhad Pasha's capture of Lori in 1584, and its season, rest on one Turkish Wikipedia article ('Serdar Ferhat Pasa'); no Armenian or scholarly confirmation located.
Lori's changes of hand between 1562 and 1734 rest on Armenian Wikipedia 'Lori berd' only.
Whether a melik house held Lori in 1584 is unverified; English Wikipedia lists Lori among provinces with melik houses but gives no date.
Season of the 643 Arab raid on Ayrarat is unverified, so snow on Ayrarat Road is license.
The relief of Artsap in Kogovit: placed in 643 by summaries of Sebeos but 'a few years' after 643 by Armenian Wikipedia; the figure of about 3,000 Arabs is low confidence.
Shirak and Kogovit as cantons of Ayrarat rest on Wikipedia 'Gyumri' and Armenian Wikipedia 'Vaspurakan', not on Hewsen's atlas.
Sebeos's smoke-and-ladders account of Dvin (640) and the 35,000 captives rest on excerpts not re-fetched; the 35,000 is a chronicle figure.
Tiglath-pileser III's personal presence at Tushpa and Sarduri's confinement there are claims of the Assyrian annals; that 735 BC was the only Assyrian approach to Tushpa rests on Radner alone.
Yeghishe's count of 1,036 Armenian dead and the 'death understood is immortality' line rest on unrefetched excerpts; translation wording varies.
Mushkan Niusalavurt commanding from an elephant rests on Kurkjian's paraphrase of Yeghishe.
Teisheba as the Urartian god of thunder and storms (for the optional Lightning subtitle) rests on Wikipedia 'Urartu' (moderate).
Use of drums by Urartian, 5th-century Armenian or 7th-century Armenian forces: unverified, so no defender tower uses drums.
Use of horns by Armenian forces in the 640s (Era 3 support tower): unverified, license.
Artillery at Avarayr, and ballistae or traction trebuchets in Armenian defence in 640-655: none recorded; all are license.
Armenian villagers owning firearms in the 1580s: unverified; the Era 4 musket tower is framed as captured weapons.
Deli serving on the eastern front in the 1580s: unverified; deli are documented as a Balkan force in the 16th century.
Local harvest timing on the Avarayr plain in late May or early June: unverified.
Freedom of worship under the Treaty of Nvarsak is a reported term (Wikipedia 'Treaty of Nvarsak', moderate); the treaty text does not survive in a source consulted here.
